speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this item was allowed to stand on Thursday last the hon. members for Van-couver-Quadra and Kootenay West were discussing the jurisdiction of the international joint commission in regard to the Columbia river reference.
I have now looked pretty carefully into the whole matter and I may give some of the conclusions to which I have come and draw the attention of members of the committee to the agreement "between the United States and Great Britain relating to boundary waters and questions arising between the United States and Canada". That agreement was signed at Washington on January 11, 1909. The articles of the treaty which outline the jurisdiction of the international joint commission are mainly articles VIII and IX. Article VIII reads for the first part as follows:
This international joint commission shall have jurisdiction over and shall pass upon all cases


involving the use or obstruction or diversion of the waters with respect to which under articles III and IV of this treaty the approval of this commission is required, and in passing upon such cases the commission shall be governed by the following rules or principles which are adopted by the high contracting parties for this purpose.
I do not at this time need to read the rules, but article VIII refers to articles III and IV. Article III deals with boundary waters and boundary waters are defined in the "preliminary article". Article III gives jurisdiction over boundary waters to the international joint commission, but may I point out right now that the Columbia river cannot be considered as a "boundary water" according to the definition of "boundary waters" which is given in the preliminary article. With the permission of members of the committee I will now read that definition:
For the purposes of this treaty boundary waters are defined as the waters from main shore to main shore of the lakes and rivers and connecting waterways, or the portions thereof, along which the international boundary between the United States and the Dominion of Canada passes, including all bays, arms, and inlets thereof, but not including tributary waters which in their natural channels would flow into such lakes, rivers, and waterways, or waters flowing from such lakes, rivers, and waterways, or the waters of rivers flowing across the boundary.
It is clear that the Columbia river and its tributaries are not boundary waters. They are not included in the general definition, and, moreover, they are excepted. They are definitely excepted by the words, and I quote:
... or the waters of rivers flowing across the boundary.
Let us examine now what could be the general jurisdiction of the international joint commission over the Columbia river, the Columbia river basin and its tributaries according to article IV. Article IV reads:
The high contracting parties agree that, except in cases provided for by special agreement between them, they will not permit the construction or maintenance on their respective sides of the boundary of any remedial or protective works or any dams or other obstructions in waters flowing from boundary waters or in waters at a lower level than the boundary in rivers flowing across the boundary, the effect of which is to raise the natural level of waters on the other side of the boundary unless the construction or maintenance thereof is approved by the aforesaid international joint commission.
That is what I said last Thursday-that if a dam was built on the other side of the border on any part of the Columbia river where it flows into the United States which would have the effect of elevating the levels of the water on the Canadian side, then the permission of the international joint commission would have to be sought. This provision

covers one of the situations which I mentioned last Thursday. If the downstream state desired to build a dam which would have the effect of raising the water level at the boundary, then the permission of the international joint commission would have to be sought. That is why an application was made to the commission in the case of the Libby dam. That application was later withdrawn so that the international joint commission did not have to adjudicate thus far on the question of the Libby dam. It was, however, clearly a case where an application had to be made to the international joint commission under article IV of the treaty.
The other article which deals with rivers flowing across the border is article II, which reads as follows:
Each of the high contracting parties reserves to itself or to the several state governments on the one side and the dominion or provincial governments on the other as the case may be, subject to any treaty provisions now existing with respect thereto, the exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent, of all waters on its own side of the line in which their natural channels would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters; but it is agreed that any interference with or diversion from their natural channel of such waters on either side of the boundary, resulting in any injury on the other side of the boundary, shall give rise to the same rights and entitle the injured parties to the same legal remedies as if such injury took place in the country where such diversion or interference occurs; but this provision shall not apply to cases already existing or to cases expressly covered by special agreement between the parties thereto.
That is another thing I said last Thursday -that unless there is a case such as the one mentioned under article IV the remedy is a legal one.
I also said that at the beginning of my remarks this afternoon that the other article of the treaty which gave general jurisdiction to the international joint commission is article IX. Article IX is the article under which the Columbia river reference has been made by the governments of the United States and Canada.
The high contracting parties further agree that any other questions or matters of difference arising between them involving the rights, obligations, or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants of the other, along the common frontier between the United States and the Dominion of Canada, shall be referred from time to time to the international joint commission for examination and report, whenever either the government of the United States or the government of the Dominion of Canada shall request that such questions or matters of difference be so referred.
The international joint commission is authorized in each case so referred to examine into and report upon the facts and circumstances of the particular questions and matters referred, together with such conclusions and recommendations as may be appropriate, subject, however, to any restrictions or exceptions which may be imposed with respect thereto by the terms of the reference.
Supply-Northern Affairs
Such reports of the commission shall not be regarded as decisions of the questions or matters so submitted either on the facts or the law, and shall in no way have the character of an arbitral award.
If it is agreeable to the members of the committee, Mr. Chairman, I would at this point ask to be allowed, with the unanimous consent of the committee, to put on Hansard the text of the Columbia river reference which was made jointly by the government of the United States and the government of Canada.

speechtext: Has the minister leave to do so?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The text of the reference is as follows:
Columbia River Reference
In order to determine whether a greater use than is now being made of the waters of the Columbia river system would be feasible and advantageous, the governments of the United States and Canada have agreed to refer the matter to the international joint commission for investigation and report pursuant to article IX of the convention concerning boundary waters between the United States and Canada, signed January 11, 1909.
2.	It is desired that the commission shall determine whether in its judgment further development of the water resources of the river basin would be practicable and in the public interest from the points of view of the two governments, having in mind (a) domestic water supply and sanitation, (b) navigation, (c) efficient development of water power, (d) the control of floods, (e) the needs of irrigation, (f) reclamation of wet lands, (g) conservation of fish and wildlife; and (h) other beneficial public purposes.
3.	In the event that the commission should find that further works or projects would be feasible and desirable for one or more of the purposes indicated above, it should indicate how the interests on either side of the boundary would be benefited or adversely affected thereby, and should estimate the costs of such works or projects, including indemnification for damage to public and private property and the costs of any remedial works that may be found to be necessary, and should indicate how the costs of any projects and the amounts of any resulting damage be apportioned between the two governments.
4.	The commission should also investigate and report on existing dams, hydroelectric plants, navigation works, and other works or projects located within the Columbia river system in so far as such investigation and report may be germane to the subject under consideration.
5.	In the conduct of its investigation and otherwise in the performance of its duties under this reference, the commission may utilize the services of engineers and other specially qualified personnel of the technical agencies of Canada and the United States and will so far as possible make use of information and technical data heretofore acquired by such technical agencies or which may become available during the course of the investigation, thus avoiding duplication of effort and unnecessary expense.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have just one more question, Mr. Chairman. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext:
May I refer the hon. member to section 4 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, which is chapter 193 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, and which reads as follows:
4.	(1) No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site thereof has been approved by the governor in council, nor unless such work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with plans and regulations approved or made by the governor in council.
(2) The provisions of this section do not apply to small wharves or groynes or other bank or beach protection works, or boat-houses, if in the opinion of the Minister of Public Works
(a)	they do not interfere with navigation, and
(b)	do not cost more than one thousand dollars.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then no one could give the green light to go ahead without the approval of the governor in council in such a case. Am I correct in that understanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Anyone who wants to build any work or have it placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water has to obtain permission from the governor in council.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Since this item was under discussion in the committee, those of us who are members of the external affairs committee have had the opportunity of hearing a thorough and comprehensive report on the whole Columbia river basin from General Mc-Naughton, who is chairman of the Canadian section of the joint commission. I believe the situation is that there has been this reference to the joint commission, and that the minister's department is merely conducting surveys,
[Mr. Lesage.1
borings and investigations on the Columbia river system within Canada on behalf of the Canadian section of the joint international commission. Is that the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is right, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is unlikely that any such thing as a dam across the Arrow lakes would be permitted until there had been a report from the international joint commission. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The waters resources of the Columbia river on the Canadian side, as far as the development of power is concerned, come under the jurisdiction of the British Columbia government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That may be so. But under the Navigable Waters Protection Act the dominion government has the power to prevent any such dam being built on the Arrow lakes which are really only a broadening out of the Columbia river. Is that not the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes; that is the case. The only thing is this. I do not believe I should be asked to answer the question: Could we use section 4 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act to prevent the building of a dam if there was no difficulty as to navigation and if the only reason we had to withhold permission was the fact that we did not have a complete report on the Columbia river reference? I do not believe I should be asked to answer that question. That would be asking me to state government policy on a matter which has not been envisaged. It is extremely difficult to give a legal opinion on these matters involving jurisdiction as between provincial and federal governments and involving the application of international law without having in front of us the complete details of the facts-a thing we do not have now because the situation has not arisen.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Canadian section of the international joint commission is, in effect, acting as the agent for both the Canadian government and the British Columbia government in conducting this investigation, so that for all practical purposes there is no way in which any difficulty can arise?

speechtext:
I understand this item includes the cost of a head office and field staffs engaged in the administration of mining, land and timber matters in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and also some land matters in the provinces. It is hard to figure out "how much is to be spent where". However, I note that there is in this item an increase over last year of $70,783 which seems to be taken up mostly by increases in salaries. There has been an increase in mining business in the Yukon Territory during the past two years. Important mineral finds have been made in many places throughout the Yukon and thousands of claims have been staked. The Yukon has every appearance of being on the threshold of mining developments of importance not only to the Yukon but to the economy of Canada. I have no hesitation in saying that if these mineral finds had been made in the older and less remote parts of Canada where better transportation facilities are available and where transportation costs are lower, many new mines would have been in operation today. I am sure that the minister knows and appreciates these things and will keep them in mind when considering improvements in transportation facilities and in strengthening the administrative staff in line with these important mineral developments. I understand that the minister and the deputy minister intend to visit the Yukon next summer. I can assure them of a most cordial welcome. I hope they will be afforded every opportunity to visit some of the more important developments which mean so much to the Yukon in particular and Canada in general. I am sure also that the minister realizes the needs of these northern areas and that the people expect encouragement and help from the federal government. They have every confidence that the minister will rectify the situation in due course.
The cost of living in the Yukon is from 30 to 75 per cent higher than south of the 60th parallel of latitude, and the scale of wages in effect in the Yukon does not compensate for the high cost of living. This fact is recognized by the government as federal civil servants in the Yukon are paid, in addition
Supply*-Northern Affairs to their salaries, a living or subsistence allowance of $1,500 per year for a married employee and $900 per year for a single employee. I would suggest that provision should be made to allow a greater exemption by way of personal income tax deductions which would offset this condition to some extent.

Much of the rest of the Arctic sea's bottom is mountainous too. The Russians said that earth folds run across it from eastern Siberia to Elies-mere island, north of Canada. They did not say how they got this information; presumably they did it by echo-sounding through the Arctic ice or through holes cut in it.
The point I wish to make is that the article says that Ellesmere island is north of Canada. It is my understanding that Ellesmere island is a part of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is also a map here indicating the same thing, that Ellesmere island is north of Canada. I am wondering whether there is any action that could be taken by the minister with respect
IMr. Fraser (Peterborough) .1

to this article. It might be a good idea for him to draw to the attention of the editors of Time that Ellesmere island is part of Canada. This sort of thing, if allowed to go without comment, could possibly lead to difficulty in the years ahead. I believe that these Arctic islands are going to prove of great value to this nation. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for the Yukon is aware of government policy with respect to road building in the Yukon. Since 1951 we have classified the roads according to three types. One is trunk roads, then secondary roads and resources roads. As to secondary roads, of course, they all come under the jurisdiction of the territorial
Supply-Northern Affairs government. There are those which are within the area or territory of one given community.
The trunk roads are those connecting various settlements. The responsibility for their construction and maintenance is borne by the territorial government but in some cases, as I believe the hon. member is aware, the federal government agrees to pay a portion of the construction and/or maintenance. As to resources roads, the capital and maintenance is borne by the federal government or it is divided between the federal government and private interests in the Yukon who are developing a mine or, we hope, water resources in that country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I interrupt the minister? Is there any federal assistance combined with territorial assistance to help a private mine in the construction of what could be classified as a mining road?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There has been some help with construction, yes. There is one instance that comes to my mind at this time, where we participated in the construction on the condition that the company would look after maintenance.
As I said the other day when talking about the problems of transportation in the Northwest Territories, after the problems of education and health, which are basic of course, the main problem that we have to deal with in the Yukon and Northwest Territories is transportation. One of the factors, if not the main factor, in the high cost of living in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, is the cost of transportation. As I said the other day, the officials of my department are now going into that question very thoroughly. This problem may be less difficult in the Yukon than it is in the Northwest Territories because of the outlet we have to these via Whitehorse and Skagway. I can assure the hon. member for the Yukon that there is nothing more to the forefront of my mind that the development of the north country, and since the transportation problem is one that we have to cope with mainly for economic development it is one to which I have given and will give the highest priority. For example, the hon. member has drawn my attention to the possibility of building a road from Carmacks along the Little Salmon river to the Pelly river and we are at present considering that possibility. I hope we can come to the conclusion for which my hon. friend hopes and have an amount in the supplementary estimates which will make the survey of the road possible this year. Of course, we have to be careful, for there have been instances in the past where we have

Such a balance is difficult to keep at times, but I can assure my hon. friend and all members of the committee that I am working hard on these matters in view of the need for development of the north country, and they may rest assured that I would be the last one to cause any delay. The brief goes on to indicate that the biggest problem faced in that province is protection from fire, yet they have not been able to reach any agreement with the dominion government on this particular activity. The federal-provincial agreement of 1951 makes no provision, however, for federal participation in financing fire protection, which is the primary problem affecting the conservation of the forest resources of British Columbia.
Such participation is essential and is warranted by the national interest in the protection and development of a basic natural resource which is a major factor in national production, national income and federal tax revenues.
Accordingly, it is submitted that the government of Canada should now enter into an agreement with British Columbia for equal financial participation in an approved plan to provide adequate protection of the forest resources of the province.

speechtext: How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Sixty-six per cent complete as of the 31st of March. Now, of course, I know of the brief to which my hon. friend refers and which was presented to the Canadian government. On the evening of the day when the premier of British Columbia presented his brief to the cabinet I had a long discussion with him, his finance minister, Mr. Gunderson, and my deputy minister, in my office. We discussed the possibility of putting into application, not only for the province of British Columbia but for all provinces, that section of the Canada Forestry Act which deals with assistance to the provinces for forest fire protection. Since then I can assure members of the committee, and particularly my hon. friend who is from British Columbia, that we have that possibility under very active consideration. It is a difficult question and I have gone into the details of many possibilities. We are still working on it and I cannot say any more at this time than that it is presently under very active consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The department has in mind entering into agreements with the provinces covering fire protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Of course, I am studying all the possibilities; but the decision to put into application that part of the forestry act is a matter of government policy and I would not be in a position today to announce what government policy on that score will be.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Forestry operations division-
334. To provide for a contribution to the province of New Brunswick for assistance in a program designed to combat the spruce budworm infestation, in accordance with an agreement entered into by Canada and the province, $500,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I just wanted to make a few comments on this item which affects my province particularly. I also want to say a word in appreciation of this vote.
This is a very important matter as far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned. Possibly hon. members may not just know what the situation has been in our province in the last few years with respect to the budworm. The budworm as a forestry pest is not something new but its ravages in the last few years have become worse than they were in previous years.
Supply-Northern Affairs
In 1951, as the minister will recall, the government of New Brunswick and the International Pulp and Paper Company decided that the situation was so serious that they would organize some scheme to see if they could eradicate this pest. In that year the government of New Brunswick and the International Pulp and Paper Company agreed to spray and did spray some 200,000 acres of spruce forests in the northern part of the province. In 1953 they found that the results had been so good that it was decided to cover more territory. The provincial government at that time organized what was known as the forest protection company. The New Brunswick government and four private companies, International Pulp and Paper Company of New Brunswick, Fraser Lumber Company, Irvine Lumber Company and Bathurst Power and Paper Company combined. To show you how extensive the work is, five airplane landing fields were constructed in the area and in that year over 1,800,000 acres of forest lands were sprayed with DDT and some sort of oil solvent which was found to be very satisfactory.
In 1954, that is this year, I understand there are to be two more airfields added to the five which have already been constructed. There are also, I believe, some 50 aircraft to be in operation. Hon. members will understand just how extensive this operation is when I say there are 50 aircraft being used, seven airfields and many hundreds of employees. I just thought I would call this matter to the attention of the house because it is not something which concerns only the province of New Brunswick. It is something which concerns the whole of Canada, and the neighbouring state of Maine is also very much concerned over the situation.
I would also like to ask the minister in connection with this item why there has been a decrease from $1 million in 1953-54 to $500,000 in 1954-55, and whether it is the opinion of his department that the situation is well under control and possibly does not require the larger amount? In this connection, if I may, I should also like to read from a report which appeared in one of our papers recently with regard to the anti-budworm operations. It reads in part as follows:
The plan is to cover new ground where the epidemic is reaching the critical stage, southeast of last year's operation. It aims to destroy the spruce budworm which, if left unchecked, could cause a major economic disaster.
Then Mr. Vernon E. Johnson, president of Forest Protection Limited, the company that was set up, had this to say in his report:
"Achievements of the last two years in the New Brunswick 'battle of the budworm' are of tremendous importance to the Canadian forest," . . .
4686	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs
Not to the New Brunswick forest particularly but to the Canadian forest, Mr. Chairman. The quotation continues:
"We now consider it economically feasible to keep five or six thousand square miles of valuable and productive forests alive for as long as we have to, to save them from destruction by an insect epidemic".
In this connection I should also like to ask the minister whether this infestation has spread to other parts of Canada, and just what the general situation is with reference to the budworm in the province of New Brunswick and in Canada generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for drawing this vote to the attention of the members of the committee because I believe what we call the budworm operation is one of the largest operations of its kind ever attempted in the world. As a matter of fact, in 1953 the spraying operations were carried on by a corporation which was set up for this purpose, namely Forest Protection Limited. As my hon. friend knows, the federal government is supplying one-third of the expenditure, the provincial government one-third and the interested company or companies one-third. Last year nearly
1.100.000	gallons of DDT insecticide were sprayed from 77 aircraft over approximately
1.800.000	acres in New Brunswick.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Seventy-seven aircraft?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Seventy-seven aircraft last year; 50 is the figure for this coming year. According to the reports I have obtained of the work done last year, subsequent studies by forest entomologists of the federal Department of Agriculture showed that the average mortality of budworm larvae from spraying ranged from 87 to 99 per cent. Enough foliage was left on the trees to justify plans for respraying only a small part of that area this year. However, there is no evidence of a decline of the budworm in unsprayed areas and plans have been made by Forest Protection Limited to spray in 1954 an additional area of about one million acres, the forest on which is now threatened. This is, of course, the reason for the cut in the expenditure. The interested companies have judged that this year they would spray only one million acres instead of 1,800,000 acres. After an interview with Mr. Johnson, the president of New Brunswick International Paper Company who is also the president of Forest Protection Limited, it was agreed that an item in the estimates of half a million dollars would be sufficient for the operation this year.
My hon. friend has asked me about the situation with regard to the budworm menace in other provinces. I know that the menace


exists in the province of Quebec and I have read in the papers that the government of Quebec would come into the picture, together with the interested companies, to do some spraying operations in eastern Quebec. This government was not asked to participate.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Quebec is spraying?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have seen in the papers a report to that effect. No assistance was requested from this government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member for Royal has covered this subject much better than I could do it, but there is one supplementary question I should like to ask the minister. Are these agreements entered into year by year or are they for any specific term? I notice that this year the amount is half a million dollars. Is there assistance for the next year under the agreement or is the agreement entered into as the case arises?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there has been an agreement between the Canadian government, the government of New Brunswick and-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Forest Protection
Limited?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, not Forest Protection Limited. It is between the two governments. As far as the Canadian government is concerned, it has relations with the government of New Brunswick, not with the companies themselves which deal with the provincial government. As far as we are concerned, the assistance is given to the provincial government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In money?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The province administers it?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No; Forest Protection Limited administers it. It is a company which has been organized on the provincial level. We have agreed to pay the government of New Brunswick-and we make our payments; we make our payments to the government of New Brunswick-one-third of the cost, up to a maximum of $3 million, of the aerial spraying operations against the budworm during the period from September 30, 1952, to March 31, 1956. Last year our contribution was $1 million. This year it will be $500,000. That is one-half of the total of $3 million which will have been spent, as far as we are concerned, at the end of the present fiscal year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister has made
reference to an offer or an arrangement the government have made with the government of the province of New Brunswick. I think he also mentioned the fact that Quebec has not asked for any assistance or taken part in any arrangements. Would that same offer be open to the province of Ontario?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We will give the hon. member's province some budworms so that they may get this assistance; they can have ours.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: We have no request from Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The reason I asked that question is this-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order. The item deals with New Brunswick, and I am afraid that we cannot, under this particular item, discuss problems relating to Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am going to discuss a problem relating to the Dominion of Canada. It is like the measles. It spread from New Brunswick across the province of Quebec into the province of Ontario. The dieback in birch is as bad now in the province of Ontario, I think, as it ever was in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member please confine his remarks to item 334 which deals with budworm in the province of New Brunswick?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Where there is a vote for a forest pest of this kind, which originated in New Brunswick and when that forest pest has now spread to Ontario, surely an hon. member is entitled to rise and to suggest that the department should make some arrangement to deal with the pest in the other provinces. To try to prevent discussion of that kind seems to me to be limiting it altogether too much.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not know how to answer the question. We do not know where this budworm started. Maybe it came from Ontario. I do not know. According to my information, it is carried by the wind over long distances. The request for assistance in this case came from New Brunswick and, as I said a few moments ago, the same situation so far as the budworm is concerned exists in eastern Quebec, but no request for assistance has been received by the federal government from the government of Quebec. The same applies to Ontario, but up to this time I have not heard of any budworm menace in Ontario.
Supply-Northern Affairs

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to enlighten the minister. I can quite understand he is new in the department, but I should like to point out that the budworm menace started in the maritimes, has also resulted in the destruction of about half the timber in Quebec and is very prevalent in the province of Ontario. We also have another menace that came from New Brunswick. We have the dieback affecting birch trees. It is very detrimental to such trees in the province of Ontario at the present time. Where winds blow across provincial boundaries I think that the dominion government cannot help but accept some responsibility.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think I must deny the statement that all these diseases come from the province of New Brunswick. Mr. Johnson, president of Forest Protection Limited, said in his report:
Achievements of the last two years in the New Brunswick "battle of the budworm" are of tremendous importance to the Canadian forest.
I should like to point out that this item does not only benefit the forests of the province of New Brunswick. The destruction of the pest in New Brunswick is keeping it from spreading to other parts of Canada which is probably of immeasurable benefit to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. As it is a national problem, we are certainly entitled to consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It has probably helped to drive it out of New Brunswick and into the other provinces.

Item agreed to.
Forest products laboratories division-
337.	Grant to Canadian Forestry Association, $10,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am very pleased that the government has recognized the good work being done by the Canadian Forestry Association by raising the grant from $6,000 to $10,000 annually.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Item agreed to.
338.	Grant to Pulp and Paper Research Institute of Canada, $100,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Would the minister explain this item? I know that in the hardwoodgrowing areas of the province of Ontario we are confronted with the fact that after the log is cut and utilized we have quite a problem in some instances in marketing the top part of the tree. I have been informed that the research council or the pulp and paper institute has been conducting research into the matter of utilizing hardwood in the manufacture of pulp and paper. Has the minister any information concerning how much progress has been made along that
4688	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs line? Would he also say whether this matter comes under the provincial government or is it the federal government that is carrying on the research work?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Eastern Rockies forest conservation board-
339.	Remuneration and expenses of federal members of the board, $12,350.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Those of us who are privileged to represent the western section of the province of Alberta have no hesitation at all in supporting the appropriation for this board. My own constituency extends to the border of British Columbia and embraces substantially what is known as the foothills area. I have no criticism whatever to offer. In fact I rise merely to suggest that in my opinion the board is doing a most excellent type of work. In the first place I should like to inquire whether there is any publication available setting forth the actual work of the board and its aims and objectives. In the second place, as a result of the number of questions directed to me by residents of that section of Alberta I wonder whether the board has given adequate consideration to its public relations. I am thinking, for example, in terms of the odd radio broadcast in that section of Alberta.
We all know that in matters of conservation of this kind in particular public understanding and co-operation are most essential. I do not make these remarks by way of criticism in any sense at all because I have no grounds for criticizing the work of the board. I simply commend them for what they are doing, but I do wonder whether the press and radio are used enough to keep people fully informed about the actual work of the board and what it intends to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: An annual report is published by the board which is tabled every year in the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was thinking more in terms of the public being informed. I am only judging from the number of questions directed to me. The people of my area know, for example, that a road is being constructed through the district. Many of them do not seem to realize the purpose of the road, although I do. Of course I get the annual report, but so far as public relations are concerned I think it would be a fine thing if the board would take under advisement the possibility of slightly better public relations in that section of Canada.
[Mr. McBain.l

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member's suggestion is that we should spend more money on public relations?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I realize that criticism has been advanced from time to time, but I have never criticized. I will support any legitimate expenditure, and I certainly think that would be most legitimate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Canadian government travel bureau-
340.	To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada, $1,561,407.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have in my hand a copy of the report of the department for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953. I should like to refer to the section dealing with the activities of the Canadian government travel bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What page?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Page 129. Under the heading "Functions of travel bureau" there is the following:
The Canadian government travel bureau is the federal agency responsible for the promotion of travel to and within Canada and for the interests of the tourist industry in general.
It is the words "in general" that I want to use as my text. I have followed the advertising of the Canadian government travel bureau in the United States and Canada considerably, and while I admit the excellent work done by the bureau in general I have come to the conclusion that the advertising tends to direct tourists, particularly those from the United States, to those areas served by the hotels operated by the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways. I would judge from the advertising that possibly the officials of these large organizations meet with the Canadian government travel bureau director and assist in planning the advertising. This is my point. I quite agree that this advertising should take place in order to bring to the attention of tourists these valuable hotel and resort facilities, but I do not think the small operators should be overlooked. There are thousands of small resort owners and I am of the opinion that they have been overlooked to some extent by the Canadian government travel bureau. For instance, Mr. Chairman, I live in one of the most beautiful districts in Canada, an area full of loveliness, as British Columbia generally is.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yet I have not seen a line of advertising about my district in United States periodicals and magazines. There are

dozens of very nice tourist resorts in British Columbia generally that are situated on small lakes or in the mountains, but the attention of tourists is not directed to the efforts of these smaller operators to provide recreational facilities for tourists. I suggest to the minister that more attention should be paid by the Canadian government travel bureau to bringing to the attention of tourists the thousands of small resorts we have in Canada, in some cases in isolated places, resorts that people prefer to go to rather than to the larger hotels. I remember on one occasion speaking to the general manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway in British Columbia, not the present general manager but a former general manager. I spoke about that steamer service that I have mentioned several times this session, Mr. Chairman. He told me that the policy of the company, so far as that service was concerned, was to make certain that the tourists proceeded along the main line of the C.P.R. and stopped at Banff, Lake Louise, the Vancouver hotel in Vancouver, and then proceeded on to Victoria and so on. We do not expect the railways to advertise the smaller resorts. I believe the Canadian government travel bureau should do more advertising of these small resorts and delightful spots to which people would go in larger numbers if they were directed to them. I should like to hear the minister's comments on my very mild criticisms and suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to be sure, first of all, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member has not taken for advertisements of the travel bureau in the United States the numerous and expensive advertisements of the railway companies and large hotels that are advertising in the United States. So far as the travel bureau is concerned, it is accomplishing a difficult job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
We have to be very careful to try to give an equal amount of advertising to all parts of Canada, and Canada is a large country with a tremendous number of beautiful resorts and wonderful places to which tourists can go. Then, too, we advertise our national parks in the United States. We are advertising the beautiful spots that we have all across the country on a basis that is as fair as we can achieve. Again it is a difficult task.
Each year we have a federal-provincial conference on tourism. Last year in the early part of December I had the privilege of presiding over the federal-provincial conference on tourism. There were representatives of all the provinces, and there were no complaints 83276-297
Supply-Northern Affairs from them that the travel bureau advertising in the United States was doing more for one part of the country than it was for other parts. So far as this mild criticism by the hon. member is concerned, as to the possibility of giving more importance in advertising to some places of beauty which might have some attraction for tourists, in which there is not a large hotel, I shall certainly look into the matter. I shall investigate the possibility of giving more prominence to the places where facilities are offered by small operators.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There are a few remarks I should like to make at this time. I must say that I believe the travel bureau has been doing a fairly good job of advertising our public parks and summer resorts in Canada. In fact, they have done such a good job, our recreational places in Canada have been receiving tourists in ever-increasing numbers. As a result of that good job we are confronted with quite a few difficulties in connection with the tourist trade. I want to point out two of those difficulties confronting tourists who travel in Canada, especially as those difficulties pertain to Banff national park.
Banff national park is, of course, -the outstanding national park in Canada. One difficulty is that the travel bureau has been advertising the fishing possibilities in Banff national park. The national film board has put out pictures depicting the wonderful possibilities in this for those who like fishing. I am informed, Mr. Chairman, -that this is causing a great deal of comment from some of the tourists who come to Banff in that when they go there they find that all this high pressure advertising is not what it was cracked up to be. When they go with their fishing tackle to spend the day on some of our rivers and cannot catch any fish at all there is keen disappointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, well-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am not a
fisherman.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Acadia, who is now in the banking and commerce committee, is, and he will verify what I am saying. He is an outstanding fisherman. I am told that there are not many fish in Banff national park. I recognize that we have a fish hatchery there, but the tourists and the people who live in Banff have told me that there are not nearly enough fish to meet the demands of the tourists who go to that park. I believe something should be done about that. I should like to know
4690	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs what the minister intends to do in order to have a more adequate supply of fish in the streams and lakes so that our tourists may be assured of a reasonable amount of fish in that park.
One of the other things about which I want to speak is tourist accommodation. The fish situation is bad, but the tourist accommodation is much worse. I do not believe there is a place in Canada that is being more troubled over tourist accommodation than Banff. About two weeks ago a person who deals with tourist accommodation in Banff was visiting Ottawa. This lady came to visit me, and incidentally I took her over to see Mr. Coleman, who is in the parks administration branch at Ottawa-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; the hon. member has just touched upon the reason why he is out of order. He is talking about national parks. The complaints he is making now pertain to the national parks to such an extent that he brought this person to the national parks branch. All the items concerning the national parks branch were passed last week, and we are now dealing with the travel bureau, which has nothing to do with national parks except the advertising of them in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am speaking about tourist accommodation. I am speaking about the very thing with which this item deals.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Tourist accommodation has nothing to do with the travel bureau, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Certainly; it is as a result of the advertising done by the travel bureau that we have this problem. If we did not have the travel bureau putting out this expensive advertising, we would not be faced with this problem. As many as five hundred tourists in one night, who come to visit Banff park, have had to sleep in their cars because there was no accommodation for them. These tourists were attracted by the advertising put out under this very item.
I could not possibly be out of order in speaking about this problem as I am now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member is discussing an item which reads:
To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada.
As the hon. member knows, a great deal of this item is for promotional advertising and I feel that perhaps the point of order raised by the minister is well taken in that the hon. member had an opportunity of discussing accommodation at national parks


under a previous item. I really do not think the hon. member, under item 340, should continue discussing the matter of accommodation in national parks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on those other items I discussed matters which came under those items. On that occasion, for example, I discussed highways and so on, but this is the only place which deals with the travel bureau and advertising put out by that bureau which attracts tourists to the Banff national park, as a result of which we in Banff find ourselves in a very bad situation. Indeed, the situation is so bad that when tourists come there as a result of this advertising put out by the bureau we sometimes have as many as five hundred people who have to sleep out at night in their cars, or in the depot if they come by bus or train.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: On a point of order. Do I understand the hon. member wishes us to stop advertising in the United States?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I made no such suggestion in that regard. I am not criticizing the travel bureau particularly for putting out such advertising. What I am criticizing is the department's failure to allow the Banff residents to provide accommodation for these people who come there as a result of this advertising. We are spending over $1,500,000 on advertising under this item and that is an increase of nearly $33,000 for this year. If that extra amount is to be effective at all it will result in an increasing number of tourists visiting Banff. What will the situation be then? The people in Banff will not be able to take care of these tourists and they will have to remain parked at night on the streets and in the parks and sleep in their cars and at the depot. Surely there is no other place to discuss this particular matter than under this item. In fact, we have spent so much time on this already that I could have been finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: If the hon. member is asking me whether there is a proper place to discuss this matter then I would point out that I have already given him my ruling on this point. The proper place to discuss this is under the items dealing wtih national parks. This is essentially an advertising item and I do hope the hon. member will devote his remarks under this item to the advertising activities of the Canadian government travel bureau.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, with your permission could that item be reopened for the purpose of discussing-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Only with the committee's consent.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Then I would like to ask the minister this, Mr. Chairman. Just what plans have the government in mind to take care of the tourists who come to Banff as a result of the advertising put out across this country by the travel bureau, the expenditure for which comes under this item? It runs to over $300 million a year. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe one of the best ways to prevent tourists from coming to Canada from now on would be to circulate prints of the speech just made by the hon. member. Out of 12,941 returns only 376 people, that is to say 2-9 per cent, had complaints to make about accommodation. That is a very small proportion.

' I shall follow a different line from that of the previous speaker. It is interesting to know the bureau estimates that approximately 65,105 people visited the Yukon Territory in 1953. the number of Canadians going abroad by only about 4 million. I noticed that the amount of money spent by Canadians who go abroad to the United States and elsewhere exceeds by $36 million that spent by the people coming from the United States to Canada.

speechtext:
The balance on the tourist trade industry is not in our favour.

have some knowledge of the number of tourists from the United States coming into the various areas of the country, then we might relate them to the advertising program in the United States. I will stop at that point to see if the minister can give me an answer, and then proceed with my argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
As the hon. member has just said, we have for the past two years been experiencing a deficit in our tourist balance with the United States, if I may put it that way.
As I said a few moments ago, it was $37 million in 1952 and $25 million in 1953. In 1950 and 1951 we had surpluses in our tourist balance with the United States. The reasons that could be given for these deficits are many, but of course one is the fact that the Canadian dollar is at a premium, and it has been at a premium for the last few years, while the United States dollar was at a premium in the previous years. This encourages Canadian tourists to travel to the United States more than the United States tourists to travel to Canada. The average expenditure per United States tourist visiting Canada last year was $10.15 while the average per capita expenditure for the Canadian traveller to the United States was $13.40, if my memory serves me correctly. More Canadians went to the United States and Canadians who went to the United States spent more per capita than United States tourists who came to Canada last year.
One of the reasons for the increased numbers of Canadian travellers not only to the United States but to other parts of the
Supply

Northern Affairs world was the fair economic position in Canada-due in large part, of course, to the good administration of this government. That has been one of the reasons; and one of the other reasons, of course, has been the premium on the Canadian dollar.
With respect to the number of tourists who have visited various parts of Canada, I believe I gave some figures regarding the national parks when we were studying this part of my estimates. I do not have the numbers now before me of visitors to Canada from the United States, but I have the proportion spent by tourists in 1952 by province of entry, if that would help my hon. friend. It is a proportion based on a total of 100 per cent. Of the United States tourists' expenditures in 1952, 50-6 per cent were made in Ontario and 18-3 per cent in Quebec. I might give the figures for 1953 which may be more up to date. In that year the figures of expenditures were 51-5 per cent in Ontario; 18-6 per cent in Quebec; 14-6 per cent in British Columbia; Atlantic provinces, 8-1 per cent; Alberta, 2 [DOT] 9 per cent; Manitoba, 2 * 5 per cent; Saskatchewan, 1-8 per cent. According to my arithmetic that makes a total of 100 per cent.

I have still one or two questions on this matter but I thank the minister for the information which he has supplied up to this point.
In commenting on his statement about Canadians going into the United States and the reasons therefor, I would say he omitted one reason-that there is a better highway system in the United States than in Canada. I am well aware that in discussing highways and accommodation for tourists in this country I would be out of order at this point, but those matters do have to be taken into consideration in respect to tourist traffic because they are of vital importance to those touring the country.
My reason for asking about the distribution of tourists throughout the different provinces, which the minister has answered by means of giving the expenditure of money, was to relate those figures to the advertising of Canada in the United States. I note in the report of the department on page 129, at the bottom of the page, that the tourist bureau operates a ground floor information office in New York, maintains an information office at Chicago, and another one at Los Angeles. Perhaps on the basis of the figures given it is a proper distribution for main offices under that arrangement. On the other hand, on a rather extensive tour that I took last summer in the United States I met a great many people who, noting that I had a Canadian licence, said, "Oh, I have been to Canada."
4694	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs I asked what part of Canada and invariably it was some place in Ontario. They were not too well informed about the other parts of Canada.
I appreciate the difficulty there is in informing people in the United States with regard to Canada, and there are very good reasons for that. However, it may be that our publicity through the travel bureau is not reaching people in the United States to the extent that we perhaps think it ought to-and it may be that certain areas of our country get more emphasis than others. I would think that in the mid-west states there should be more mention of the prairie provinces than there should be of Ontario and Quebec, for instance. I do not know whether that is done but I think it should be done.
I was in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and so on but I do not recall seeing at garages, tourist camps and places where we stayed any information relating to Canada in the way of literature. I could, however, find information with regard to the various states of the union. It may well be that our publicity through the travel bureau should be directed at a wider distribution of road maps at filling stations and tourist camps in various parts of the United States. A person who starts off on an automobile tour does not always have the tour planned in advance. He does not always start off with full information. He sometimes makes diversions and the diversions may occur part way through his trip. If he is able to find information about some other point of interest at a tourist camp in the state or province within which he is moving he may change his direction. That is exactly what I have done on more than one occasion when going from coast to coast. A United States tourist might very well do that if he could get information about various parts of Canada at United States tourist camps and filling stations. That might well result in increased United States tourist travel in parts of our country which are not visited to the same extent as the two central provinces are visited.
I intended to ask another question. I notice in the report, on page 132, that the seventh federal-provincial tourist conference was held on December 2 and December 3, 1952. Supply-Northern Affairs provinces not only outside of Canada but also in the other provinces of Canada. We do not do any advertising in Canada itself. speechtext: In the past few months has the minister observed the position where these advertisements are inserted in such magazines as Life, Time, the National Geographic, the Saturday Evening Post and others?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have seen some and I think they are fairly well placed in the magazine. They are pretty conspicuous. I think it is good advertising and it is well placed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask a question respecting the type of advertisement that is used. We are spending $1 million, and I should like to know whether it is general advertising that applies to all of Canada or whether we advertise certain sections of the country. I ask this question because I come from a part of the country that has a very extensive tourist trade. The county council of the county of Prince Edward, the town council of the town of Picton, and the chamber of commerce of Prince Edward county spend considerable money each year in putting out a tourist pamphlet which is sent to all parts of the United States. Of course we think it is good business to do so. What I really want to know is whether the advertising in all these publications is general in its nature; or is some part of Canada advertised as being better than others?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: In the national magazines the advertising is general. In the magazines I have mentioned the advertising is for Canada as a whole. However, so far as advertising in newspapers is concerned, we may at times advertise a region like the maritime provinces in a New York paper and advertise Manitoba or central Canada in a Chicago paper. That would apply to newspapers, but as far as magazines are concerned the advertising is of a general character applying to the whole of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Who designs these advertisements? Are they designed wholly by the advertising agency, or are the designs submitted by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

They are designed by the
agency, Cockfield Brown, under the direction of the director of the travel bureau who, as my hon. friend knows, has quite a lot of experience in that field.

I am sure he will be satisfied, as I must be because I come from Quebec, that Canada does not end at Montreal.
