speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
In presenting the estimates of my department, Mr. Chairman, I have for the past few years given a short statement in which I have reviewed the estimates according to the summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories, which is inserted at the back of the estimates book. In my statement I called attention to the major projects and attempted, in the time at my disposal, to explain the more significant changes. Inasmuch as such a review seems to have been of assistance to hon. members, I propose, if it meets with the approval of the committee, to follow the same practice this year.
Before turning to an examination of the needs of the Department of Transport proper, I wish to point out that the estimates of the department, the air transport board, the board of transport commissioners, the Canadian maritime commission and the national harbours board aggregate $135,212,000 for 195455, roughly $13 million more than in 1953-54. The estimated net expenditure for the department alone in 1954-55 is $123,635,041, an increase of $14,678,972 over last year, mainly on account of the four following items.
First, civil salaries and wages, where the increase is $2,600,000. This was to give effect to the general salary revision which took place effective on December 1, 1953. Then, in construction and acquisition of buildings

and works, there is an increase of, roughly speaking, $2 million. Most of this increase is due to the celerity with which work has progressed on the Canso causeway. The third item has to do with construction or acquisition of equipment, $1,400,000, and there the increase arises mainly from the construction of vessels for the department.
Then under the heading of contributions, grants, and subsidies, there is an increase of $7,478,000, which is due chiefly to the decision of the government to implement one of the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation, namely, that which recommended a subsidy of $7 million for the maintenance of the railway tracks of the two main railways of Canada over the bridge which extends between the head of the lakes and eastern Canada. The increases in the estimates for this year therefore are in the main explained by the figures I have just given.
In addition to our own commitments my department will carry out services for the Department of National Defence such as air traffic control, meteorological services at establishments operated by the R.C.A.F., army, navy, or the defence research board, and construction and operation of facilities required under the NATO plan, estimated to cost $2,500,000.
Under object 1, that is salaries and wages, which amount roughly to $33 million, we have been obliged to provide for an increase of approximately $2,600,000. As I indicated, the greater portion of this, some $1,900,000, is required to cover the general salary increases to government employees authorized in November of last year. The balance is due to normal changes such as reclassifications, promotions and annual increases.
Here I would like to say a word or two about the number of employees in the Department of Transport because I know from time to time there is criticism in the house over the increase or decrease, though mostly that criticism is directed to the increases, in the number of employees in the department.
The total number of employees in the department at this time is 11,129. This is a reduction of 229 from last year and 412 from the year 1952-53. As is to be expected, this decrease is a net figure. By that I mean there are increases in certain units of the department and offsetting decreases in others. For example, in canal services there is an increase of 84 operating positions on the main line canals authorized to permit a six-day work week; in steamer operations we will need 44 positions for a new supply and 83276-2981
Supp ly-Transport
buoy vessel at Saint John, New Brunswick; a reduction of 56 appears in aids to navigation, due chiefly to electrification of minor lights. In the telecommunications division, the sale of our facilities in British Columbia, coupled with the abolition of the private radio receiving station licence, results in a decrease of 385, but some 44 extra employees were needed to staff Loran stations in Newfoundland taken over from the U.S. coastguard, and new marine radio stations at Channel Head and Bicquette.
In the field of civil aviation there are 100 positions less, although in that sphere we contemplate no major changes in the general pattern of operation of airports. My department continues to be responsible for 102 airports and landing fields, although I am glad to say there have been signs of increasing municipal interest, with the cities of Sudbury and Timmins taking over operation of new municipal airports. We have agreed to take over in 1955 the operation of the airport at Vancouver which is the major Canadian international terminal on the west coast. At the present time negotiations are under way with the city of Vancouver with reference to the actual possession of the site, but I am informed by the city authorities that another plebiscite is required sometime in the near future and that it will not be possible to take over the airport until after that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext: What is the price that has been agreed upon?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
One million dollars. I will skip for the time being several of the objects such as civilian allowances and professional and special services, there having been decreases in the latter, and move on to object No. 5, travelling, transportation and removal expenses. Here there is a decrease of $21,381 due largely to the sale of the British Columbia government telegraph and telephone system. I might say at this point that the sale of these facilities to private or semiprivate enterprises is in accordance with the government's policy of disposing of public enterprises to commercial interests wherever it is economically feasible to do so.
The bulk of our travel and removal expense is chargeable to the air services branch. The nature of the duties performed by the civil aviation, telecommunications, meteorological and engineering divisions necessarily calls for a great deal of travel on inspection duties, and the transportation of people to and from the arctic, the subarctic and isolated points in Canada. Bxperience has shown that it is inadvisable to leave an

Supply-Transport
employee for more than two years in isolation. It has been our experience, too, that young men of this generation insist on getting married and taking their wives and families with them. Feeling this, it is next to impossible to fill these posts. The price, therefore, is what we pay for operating isolated stations in the middle of the twentieth century, in spite of which we have, by careful scrutiny, managed to show a slight decrease this year.
With reference to object No. 8, telephones, telegrams and other communication services, there is an increase here of $93,397 which results chiefly from the operation of the national facsimile circuit. That circuit was put into operation last year for the defence services and it is operated at Dorval. It is a system by means of which it is possible to improve weather observation programs in northern Canada, and it is a direct outgrowth of the defence program. It will help in giving a better weather reporting service and better general knowledge as to the climate.
These increases are due also to new weather reporting stations which will be operated at places such as Baker Lake, Fort Nelson, Aklavik and Coppermine. In rendering those services, either for the Department of National Defence or for the public generally, the leasing of wire facilities is essential to the rapid transmission of meteorological data.
I think I can leave that item for the moment and come to a major item which I know is of interest to this house, and that is object No. 13, construction or acquisition of buildings and works, including land. The amount in the estimates this year under this object is $33,741,791, and I should like to give the committee an outline of the major works or programs under way or projected, and in so doing I shall deal with the operating branches in the order in which they appear in the estimates.
In canal services there is a reduction of $1,280,000. This is due to the fact that the Atwater avenue and St. Remi tunnel installations will be practically completed.
As a matter of fact, I should have said the St. Remi development has been completed and the Atwater tunnel, now practically complete, is expected to be opened officially some time next month.
The Atwater avenue project embodies two double-lane vehicular-controlled access roadways 24 feet 6 inches in width and 2,400 feet in length extending from the intersection of Notre Dame street and Atwater avenue north of the Lachine canal to Centre street and Atwater avenue south of the canal, carried under the waterway in a tunnel 787 feet in length.
[Mr. Chevrier.l
The tunnel proper consists of two tubes in each of which is provided a two-lane roadway as well as a 6-foot pedestrian sidewalk. The most modern lighting, ventilating and pumping equipment has been installed. The Atwater avenue project was constructed at a cost of approximately $6,750,000, and the St. Remi project, a somewhat similar installation, cost $4,500,000.
Under aids to navigation there is one large project, namely the second stage of the work involved in the construction of a 60-foot diameter lighthouse pier, with machinery and equipment, off the lower end of White Islet reef, some 80 miles below Quebec city. The amount of $600,000 is included for this work.
Under the strait of Canso improvements, since it is anticipated that this project will be 85 per cent complete by the end of March, 1955, we are placing in the estimates this year an amount of approximately $10 million, or $9,670,000, to be exact, which is $3 million in excess of last year's commitment. The committee will recall that the principal features are the rock-fill causeway across the strait, the ship lock on the Cape Breton shore, together with the necessary construction and relocation of railway trackage and highways. Here I may say that I visited the causeway not many months ago and flew over it. I was able to see for myself the excellent progress which was made at the time. In fact, the work by the contractor, the Northern Construction and J. W. Stewart Limited, is considerably ahead of schedule. There are three contracts involved there, the one for the construction of the causeway which has been awarded to the contractor whose name I have just mentioned, and the contract for the navigation lock, which was awarded to T. C. Gorman Limited, a subsidiary of Canadian Dredge and Dock, in March, 1953, at a cost of $5 million, roughly speaking. Here, too, the firm has made excellent progress.
The other contracts were awarded to the Maritime Steel and Foundries Limited of New Glasgow for the fabrication and erection of a combined highway and railway bridge across the upper entrance of the ship lock and for the sector gates of the lock.
Contracts for grading railway diversions have been awarded to the Modern Construction Company and Wasson Construction Company.
Then, dealing with the North Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry terminals, the terminal facilities at North Sydney include a pier 800 feet long by 163 feet wide, to provide on one side a berth for the William Carson, a vessel which was recently launched at the yards of Vickers in Montreal, and on the other side

berths will be provided for the Canadian National Railways who will be operating the ferry. There is also a large transit shed with a floor space of some 100,000 square feet which is under construction. The contract for the pier and shed foundation was awarded to T. C. Gorman Limited; for the structural steel frame of the transit shed to Robb Engineering Works Limited, and for other work on the shed to A. F. Byers Construction Company Limited.
The total estimated expenditure at North Sydney is in the neighbourhood of $3,900,000.
Then the facilities at Port aux Basques; wharf and other facilities are to cost $7 million, of which $2,250,000 is being provided in these estimates. We are also providing for the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor terminal. The Department of Public Works will undertake the construction of a dock together with the requisite terminal facilities at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. An amount of $1 million is included in this year's estimates to provide for a loan to the Canadian National Railways to be applied to the construction of dock and terminal facilities at Bar Harbor, Maine. The town of Bar Harbor has provided a free site, and the state of Maine is advancing $1 million, subject to annual repayment without interest over a period of 30 years toward the construction.
I now deal with telecommunications. It accounts for more than $3 million of the object with which I am dealing. Some of the more important activities proposed for this field of operations are the continuation of the program for the installation of the new type of radio range system. It is a visual range between Montreal on the east and Windsor on the west. There is also provision for a ground control approach system at Gander to serve transatlantic flying; construction of radio range at lac Eon, reactivating radio range station at Fort Chimo, construction of radio range at Terrace to assist Kitimat aluminum development.
Under the meteorological heading there is construction for the meteorological division, owing to increased work in the north, and the major expenditures for this purpose have to do with the development of rawinsonde stations at Coral Harbour, Coppermine, Baker Lake and Nitchequon. This is an advanced form of weather observation through the use of balloons carrying equipment which sends back radio signals, giving a wide variety of detail on weather and wind conditions at various altitudes. It is a part of a general program to ensure complete weather coverage of northern Canada for defence purposes.

Under the heading of civil aviation are our airports programs which will call for the heaviest construction for the air services branch. The proposed outlay this year is $10 million, and as opposed to last year, the accent will be on terminal buildings this time rather than on runway facilities.
I do not mean, by that, that we shall neglect runways, but we have a certain amount of money placed at our disposal, and the time has come when we have to renovate and give considerably more attention during the fiscal year to new terminal facilities. For instance, the major expenditures in this category will be made at Gander airport. The new terminal building at Saskatoon should be brought to a close. A civil terminal building at Harmon field, which is the United States base at Stephenville in Newfoundland, is proposed, provided that we can reach agreement with United States authorities. We also intend to make a start on a new and major terminal building at Dorval.
There will be as well substantial continuing work on runway development. A second runway at Gander is being lengthened and strengthened. At Windsor and lakehead, runways will be altered to accommodate the Viscount aircraft which Trans-Canada Air Lines are acquiring. Other locations I might mention are at Winnipeg, Fort McMurray, Yellowknife, Grande Prairie, Prince Albert, Rimouski, Rouyn and Quebec city.
A glance at the summary will show that we are proposing a total expenditure of approximately $13 million under the category of equipment, construction or acquisition, which is about 12 per cent over last year's figures, namely, $1,400,000 more than last year. This increase is related for the most part to the construction of vessels I mentioned earlier. I wanted to give the committee details of the construction of those vessels and I do so now, because I know the committee will be interested in this construction, which accounts for approximately $10 million of the $13 million referred to earlier.
The funds with reference to these are allocated as follows:
(1)	a lighthouse supply and pilotage tender required at Goose Bay. The estimated cost is $90,000;
(2)	a lighthouse supply and buoy vessel at Quebec. The estimated cost is $1,100,000, but we are providing $50,000 for preliminary expenditures only this year;
(3)	a lighthouse supply and buoy vessel for Saint John, New Brunswick. The amount provided for completion of this item is $1,900,000;

(4)	a lighthouse supply and buoy vessel for Victoria, British Columbia. I explained last year that we proposed to construct this vessel at an estimated cost of $1,250,000. The sum of $800,000 is provided to cover expenditures this year;
(5)	the Pacific ocean standby weather ship, St. Stephen, is in urgent need of refitting. We have provided $400,000 for this purpose;
(6)	the ferry vessel for the North Sydney-Port aux Basques service, on which we expect to spend $2,600,000;
(7)	the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry vessel, the keel of which was laid last summer, will be ready for operation in 1955. The reports I have indicate her construction is proceeding in a very satisfactory manner, and in these estimates provision is made for the expenditure of $4,100,000.
The last vessel to be named is a ferry vessel, for which we have included an initial amount of $250,000, and which will operate between Wood Island, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia. The government has decided to undertake this construction in view of the serious need for improving the service. The estimated cost of the ship is $1,500,000.
There are a number of other items that I could deal with either generally or in detail, out I think I have given the committee a jufficient idea of what the department inbends to spend in the various divisions, namely, rail service, marine service and air service, and I think this should suffice for the purpose of the consideration of the estimates at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I do thank the minister for giving us this summary of the moneys which he asked to have voted this year, based on the summary of standard objects which has been distributed to us with the annual estimates. I often wonder why the other departments do not make use of this summary. The minister is about the only one in the cabinet who does give us the story based on that summary.
As he explained, he is asking for about $135,200,000. in rough figures. That is an increase of $13,150,000-in other words an increase of more than 10 per cent over the expenditures in the last fiscal year. This increase is the fourth largest of any of the departments and it is asked for in spite of the fact that there is a decrease in the national harbours board vote of approximately $1,730,000, and a saving to the government because of selling the government telegraph and telephone system in British Columbia of about $975,000 under the administration item and about $645,000 under the construction item. Incidentally, I am afraid that the government
[Mr. Chevrier.l
did not make a very good deal when it sold those two systems. It certainly did not get the top price or anything near it.
Referring to the standard objects, we find that most of the items have been increased. The minister mentioned briefly telephones and telegrams. They are now up for the department, as distinguished from the boards, to almost $3 million, which is a very large sum to spend for service of this kind. This year there is an increase of $90,000 over the amount in last year's estimates and I find it very hard to believe that such a large increase was necessary.
Another item which has gone up a great deal is that for office stationery. The minister did not deal with it when he spoke, but his department is to spend $659,000 for office stationery, supplies, equipment and furnishings. That is an increase over the preceding year of $105,000. I suggest to the minister that items like this are ones on which a determined effort to make reductions would be far more beneficial than the amounts involved, because it would teach thrift. It would help to spread ideas of thrift throughout the department. I do not understand why there should be that increase in this particular item.
I will next turn to repairs and upkeep of equipment. We find that item is up to $2,372,000-an increase of about $150,000. That is not for the purchase of equipment but merely for repairs and upkeep of equipment owned by the department. Then we have rentals of equipment-practically doubled this year. In fact it is more than double, it has gone from $83,000 to $190,000. The minister did not say anything about either of the last two mentioned items and I think before this first item is passed he should just explain why there are these large increases in these items.
There is an increase in the special category called deficits of $1,265,000. He did not attempt to explain that and I would ask him to do so.

He said that the staff of his department had been decreased. Well, there must be something wrong with my figures because I worked it out that he had an increase of about 165 after taking into consideration the fact that he was able to cut his staff by about 244 because of the disposal of the government telegraph and telephone system in British

Columbia. We will have to try to get together on those figures. I had intended to censure him for such a large increase under present conditions.
I have another point in connection with his estimates and it is this. I would like to know why it would not be possible to have the Department of Public Works do some of the construction work for the Department of Transport. This year the minister is asking for $33,740,000 in round figures for the construction or acquisition of buildings, works and land. That is almost one-half of the amount that we voted the Department of Public Works for the same type of expenditure-and the Department of Public Works is supposed to be the building department in this governmental set-up. When their estimates were up I pointed out that the government has been getting into the very bad habit of setting up little building branches in all other departments-and I think the Department of Transport has the largest building department outside the Department of Public Works. I do not see why much of this construction should not be brought under the Department of Public Works.
The minister referred, for example, to airways and the fact that construction of airways and airports totalled $10 million. He mentioned that his department was going to build terminal buildings. Why does the Department of Transport have to build terminal buildings at airports when the Department of Public Works builds ajl the other buildings at those particular centres? I suggest that we would economize if we had the Department of Public Works doing building of that type. I admit that there are some types of construction which can well be carried out under the Department of Transport, but I hope that during this year the minister will go through all of these construction items and see if it would not be possible to hand over some of the work to the Department of Public Works.

not build this dock at North Sydney? The same thing applies to the dock at Port aux Basques where there is a vote of $2,555,000. Then there is the meteorological service, $970,000; telegraphs and telephone, $310,000; northwest communication system, $205,000; radio aids, $516,000. There must be a lot of construction which is to be covered by those votes which could very well be done by the Department of Public Works. The minister has mentioned tunnels in Montreal to be built. Why could not the Department of Public Works build them?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext: Those are all facilities that have to do with transport. They are connected with the Canadian National Railways either directly or indirectly. I think it would be a bad principle to divide them giving a proportion to public works and a proportion to transport.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext: They may be connected with the railways but they are public works. I think the onus should be on any department to show that the Department of Public Works cannot build a particular work before a department such as the Department of Transport undertakes to do it. The national harbours board, for construction, are asking $5 million. I should like to know why some of that work cannot be done by the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
What about the St. Lawrence waterway? Is the Department of Transport going to do all the construction work on the St. Lawrence waterway and in that way become a far greater building department than is the Department of Public Works? I should like the minister to explain just what part the respective departments are going to have in the construction work that will be done on that waterway.
Another point is this. There have been great changes in the Department of Public Works. An extensive face-lifting has been going on there for the last few months. At least, we are told that is what has been happening, and I think perhaps the information is correct. I am wondering whether anything of the kind is taking place or is about to take place in the Department of Transport.
I have here an extremely interesting book called "The Canadian Bureaucracy" by Taylor Cole. It deals with Canadian government.

Supply-Transport
At page 22, referring to these two departments, namely public works and transport, we find this statement:
Certain other departments are still known as "patronage departments" in popular parlance. These include the departments of public works and transport, which have an appreciable number of "prevailing-rates" employees not subject to the jurisdiction of the civil service commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext: I had never heard that this was a patronage department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
This is the opinion of this author who wrote the book entitled "The Canadian Bureaucracy". I hope his views are incorrect. But perhaps it would not be a bad idea for the minister to take a look around his department in order to see whether that charge is a fair one. After all, his department is not free of faults.
Why does the Department of Transport not permit the opening of tenders in public? I am told that it is the only department of government that refuses to have tenders opened in public, apart from the war departments. I have here a brief of the Canadian Construction Association which was submitted to the government on February 22 of this year. In it we find this statement:
Endorsation was also given to another policy statement advocating the calling of competitive tenders on all construction work involving public funds and the public advertising and opening of these tenders except with regard to work in the "secret" or emergency categories. We are happy to report that all federal agencies conform to this policy with but one exception-
And I believe that exception is the minister's department.
-and that the procedures followed by such agencies as the Department of Public Works and the national harbours board are frequently cited as examples to other governmental bodies. During the past year, a number of departments carrying out relatively small construction programs agreed to conduct public tender openings with a representative of the association present and currently there is only one department that does not make construction tender information available. It is hoped that this situation will soon change. The privilege of attending the tender openings for federal construction projects is very much appreciated by the association in that it enables bidders to be advised quickly as to their relative standing. This information is most helpful for it enables decisions without delay concerning equipment movements and whether or not to tender on other projects. It also is a further indication to potential bidders that their tenders will be considered on an equitable basis. From the department's standpoint, public tender openings constitute good public relations and will tend to encourage greater competition and ensuing better prices for its projects.
That suggestion was made to the cabinet. I hope that the department either have already acted on it or will do so in the future.
I intend to devote the rest of my time this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, to one subject which

comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport, namely Canada's deep-sea merchant marine. We in the opposition are greatly concerned about the merchant marine. We regret that adequate steps have not yet been taken by the government to avert the disappearance of the Canadian deep-sea fleet. We believe it is not yet too late to prevent this tragedy, and we urge the government to take another look at the situation.
After world war II the government studied the problem of Canada's deep-sea fleet. We came out of the war with a substantial merchant navy; I believe we had the third or fourth largest merchant fleet in the world. As a result of the studies made, it was decided that we would have a merchant navy with modern fast ships. I have here the pertinent report of the Canadian maritime commission, namely their second report which is the one made in 1949. At page 51 they sum up this policy as fallows:
It appears to us that in the next few years Canada's chief problem will be to dispose of her exportable surpluses.
Of course, that statement is true today. The quotation continues:
It is not possible or advisable to force overseas buyers to ship in Canadian bottoms if they have not dollars to pay in freights. It is therefore obvious that the Canadian flag fleet must be drastically reduced. We believe, however, that with the advantage of trade routes developed during and since the war and under normal conditions the Canadian shipping industry has a reasonable opportunity of continuing in existence with a comparatively small well-balanced fleet composed of modern fast ships suitable for the trades in which they are employed.
I believe there was a later recommendation by the Canadian maritime commission in which they recommended to the government that there should be a nucleus of about 50 ships in the Canadian deep-sea fleet, including those ships belonging to Canadian National Steamships. I believe the recommendation also indicated that there was only one way in which such a fleet could be acquired, namely to subsidize operating expenses of, for instance, 25 or 30 ships. Apparently the cost of operating a Canadian ship is about $100,000 a year higher than that of operating a British ship. That recommendation therefore would have involved a subsidy of about $2,500,000 or $3 million.
Then I believe there was, from an interdepartmental committee known as the external trade policy committee, a recommendation to much the same effect with regard to a merchant fleet. But these recommendations have been ignored or rejected by the government. I admit that various plans, such as the tonnage-replacement plan, have been tried; but they have been unsuccessful. We now find

ourselves in a position where the Canadian merchant fleet has practically disappeared.
Mr. Chairman, at that point may I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had just commenced to deal with the question of Canada's deep-sea merchant marine and had pointed out that the government had adopted a policy shortly after the war of having a merchant navy composed of a reasonably small number of modern fast ships, but that in spite of that policy having been adopted it had failed and that we now have reached the position where the deep-sea fleet is practically gone.
The last statement of policy was made by the Minister of Transport in November of last year. It set out that the ship owners could sell their vessels but that the proceeds must be placed in the escrow fund which had been established some years earlier and must be used to buy modern cargo vessels. There was also a change in what had been followed previously in that it was provided that any new vessels need not necessarily be built in Canadian yards. That of course was designed to enable the ship owners to have their ships constructed in British yards where they could be had for a good deal lower price.
But it was stated in the policy that the government would not pay any operating subsidy at the time. The paragraph dealing with operating subsidies read as follows:
It is further announced that, after due consideration, the government has decided that the request made by the Canadian Shipowners Association for operating subsidy could not be approved at the present time. However, if it appears feasible to establish modern Canadian flag vessels on certain routes that would be of benefit to the development of Canadian trade, Mr. Chevrier indicated that consideration might be given at a later date as to whether or not some form of assistance ought to be provided in such cases.
The government also refused at the time to allow the ship owners to sell their ships outright without any conditions.
A few days later, on November 26, I spoke in the house during the debate on the speech from the throne and asked the Minister of Transport this question: Are we going to have a Canadian merchant navy or are we not? I pointed out that the sixth report of the Canadian maritime commission, dated
Supply-Transport
June 29, 1953, had shown that there only remained 65 deep-sea dry cargo vessels in the Canadian merchant fleet as of March 31, 1952. At the time I spoke in November, 1953, that number had already been reduced to 44, and it was only too clear at the time that the whole fleet was on the way out unless some drastic action was taken by the government.
The minister replied the following day, November 27, and his remarks will be found at page 410 of Hansard. He argued that the country would have to find some $100 million to $200 million if there was to be a modern cargo fleet. He based that figure on a cost of $4 million per ship and argued on the basis that the government would have to pay either the whole cost of the new ships or at least half of the cost. Nobody has ever suggested that. I have never heard it suggested by the ship owners or by anyone else. Certainly I did not suggest it. The only suggestion that had been made was that there should be an operating subsidy of $100,000 per year per ship.
Then the minister went on to argue that we had 90 ships under United Kingdom registry and that they could be brought back if we needed more ships. The facts are that those ships are all old ships. They were all built during the war, and they are manned of course by British officers and seamen. The manner in which they are used is under the direction of the British authorities. When they have major repairs done that work goes to British shipyards, and they could not be operated by Canada even if they were brought back at the present time.
I asked the minister a series of questions which were answered on February 18. The answers are to be found at page 2201 of Hansard. One of the questions was:
What plans, if any, has the government in hand to man and operate these vessels-
The reference is to the Canadian vessels which had been transferred to United Kingdom registry.
-if they should be returned to Canadian registry?
This was the answer:
In the event of the return of any or all of these vessels to Canadian registry their Canadian owners, operators or managers would man and operate them as they did in the past.
That sounds very good, but the fact is that the officers and seamen who were in the Canadian merchant navy have gone to other work. They had to leave. They had to find other jobs. I know quite a few of them in Vancouver who have given up the sea as a career and have gone into other work.

Supply-Transport
They are not available to man these ships if they should ever be brought back from the United Kingdom.
Then the minister argued that everything was all right because if there were a war there was going to be a North Atlantic Treaty Organization shipping pool and we would be taken care of out of that pool. I understand that other nations are not quite so simple. They are retaining ships which are not being placed in the pool so that they may protect their own interests. If Canada gets into the position where the only ships she may have in the pool are those that have been transferred long since to British registry-most of them have been gone quite a while-then her voice in that pool will not be very loud.
The statement of policy made by the minister on November 12 was followed by the flight of further vessels from the Canadian flag. I understand that at the time my questions were answered in February, applications had been made for the transfer of 21 more ships to British registry. Those applications have been approved. In addition I believe a few ships have been sold, but not one modern cargo vessel has been built or is about to be built as a result of this policy announced on November 12.
The position is that at the end of June Canada will have approximately 21 dry cargo deep-sea vessels in her merchant marine. Of those 21, only 14 are engaged in the deep-sea trade. Only two of the hundreds that were built during the war, 10,000-ton-ners, are engaged in foreign trade. There is one 4,700-tonner, eight Canadian National steamships and three other vessels that were built since the war, but apparently they are not fast modern cargo vessels. The eight vessels owned by Canadian National Steamships may very well be sold. The company operated at a deficit, I believe, last year, and there have been press reports to the effect that the Canadian National Steamships may go out of the freight business, in which event 8 of those 14 ships would be gone. The other 7 ships, making a total of 21, are all plying in coastal waters.
The situation can very well be illustrated by what has happened to the ships that were steaming out of the port of Vancouver. In 1947 we had 46 Canadian cargo vessels working out of that port. This year that number was reduced first to two and then to one. I believe the transfer of that one to United Kingdom registry has already been approved, and as soon as she returns from her present voyage she will go to the United Kingdom registry. The great port of Vancouver, therefore, will have no deep-sea cargo vessels under the Canadian flag.

Canada will have, at the end of June, the smallest tonnage of dry cargo vessels in 35 years. This situation, Mr. Chairman, is tragic and yet the government has no effective policy to meet it. The government is acting as though we had a fleet. I point out to the minister that in his own estimates, vote 453, we find under the particulars at page 527 there is money to be voted for a training program for the certification of able seamen, and incidentally for campaign stars and war medals for merchant seamen. These men are getting their medals a good deal more easily than they got proper benefits. Then, under vote 473 of the Department of Transport, we find there is to be $300,000 voted for degaussing and strengthening for armament sea-going merchant ships of Canadian registry of 1,000 gross tons and over. I point out that if the minister does not get this work done quickly he will not have any ships left to degauss. Then under vote 188, for the Department of Labour, the general description states that this money is to be used in part for the training of personnel for the merchant marine.
These votes are being asked, yet actually the government is just letting the Canadian merchant navy die out. As I said, officers and seamen have gone to other jobs. Canadian operators are going into other businesses. Foreign vessels are moving in, and to me this is one of the greatest failures of the present Canadian government. The official opposition believes that Canada must keep the nucleus of a deep-sea fleet, composed of at least a reasonable proportion of modem fast vessels; that we must keep a certain number of trained personnel and experienced operators. It is obvious that that should be Canadian policy, and I should like to give the committee some of my reasons for making that statement.
First of all we need a merchant marine to carry our trade. We have to export to live, and we have to export more per head than the people of any other nation. Yesterday this house approved of the Canada-Japan trade treaty. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, who is to carry that trade. It certainly is not going to go in Canadian bottoms. Japanese merchant ships are already coming into Vancouver harbour, bringing in their goods and taking away iron ore and other materials. Practically all this trade is going to be carried in Japanese bottoms unless the Canadian government changes its policy.
Then, let us consider the St. Lawrence. Here we are about to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. All of the ports on the great lakes are looking forward to a large foreign trade. There will not be very

many Canadian cargo vessels coming in with that trade. Practically all the trade that is carried in deep-sea vessels is going to be carried by foreign vessels, unless there is a change in Canadian government policy so that we do retain a Canadian merchant marine. Then, too, we should not make ourselves subject to the whims of other nations in so far as deep-sea shipping is concerned. We need a merchant navy for defence. What is the use of building a big escort fighting navy when we have not any ships to escort? That is the position in which Canada stands today.
I have here a press dispatch of June 9, 1950, reporting a speech by Vice Admiral Grant, who was then chief of the Canadian naval staff. He said:
No one has yet produced a substitute for the merchant ship . . . We should make no mistake, in the event of an attack on the freedom loving nations, we must be prepared to carry the war to the enemies' gates and the maintenance and supply of our allied forces overseas would require all the merchant shipping of the free world afloat today, plus every ton we could build.
Three months ago, on February 12, a further press dispatch appeared reporting a statement by J. A. S. Peck, naval architect with Canadian Vickers Limited. He pointed out Canada's need for a competent merchant marine in time of national emergency. He is reported as having told members at the annual meeting of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association that a merchant marine was needed, not merely to transport men and material to particular danger points but to act as the nation's economic lifeline at a time when externally-owned tonnage may be in critically short supply.
We need a merchant marine to help Canadian shipyards. The construction of naval vessels is nearing an end, and when there is no more of that work our shipyards are going to be in serious trouble. We should have Canadian merchant vessels that could keep these yards busy with repair work, and new vessels could also be built in these Canadian yards. We need a merchant marine for the retention of management and operational skills and for the prestige of the nation; for the development of Canada into one of the greatest nations of the world and because a merchant marine is part of our general transportation picture. A merchant marine is just as much a part of the transportation problem of Canada as is transportation within our boundaries; it is all part of one transportation picture.
I would point out that no other nation has followed a policy such as the one this government has now adopted. Back in 1936
Supply-Transport
the United States decided that they were going to maintain a merchant navy and in their merchant marine act of that year we find this declaration of policy set out in section 101:
It is necessary for the national defence and development of its foreign and domestic commerce that the United States shall have a merchant marine (a) sufficient to carry its domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of the water-borne export and import foreign commerce of the United States and to provide shipping service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of such domestic and foreign water-borne commerce at all times, (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency, (c) owned and operated under the United States flag by citizens of the United States in so far as may be practicable, and (d) composed of the best-equipped, safest, and most suitable types of vessels, constructed in the United States and manned with a trained and efficient citizen personnel. It is hereby declared to be the policy of the United States to foster the development and encourage the maintenance of such a merchant marine.
That policy was investigated this year by a committee set up under the under-secretary of commerce. In his report, published on May 3, we find this as his first conclusion:
Our basic national maritime policy is sound. Indeed, its objectives are so fundamental to the national interest that their attainment should be given primary consideration at all times.
Japan and Germany are moving rapidly into the field. Last year, 1953, the British built the largest tonnage of new ships, but Germany was second and not very far behind, while Japan was third. Those two countries had great merchant fleets before the war and they are rapidly getting back into the same position.
Even Switzerland has a merchant marine which will be bigger than the Canadian merchant marine at the end of June. I have here the foreign trade publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce for December 19, 1953 and in an article entitled "Switzerland's Merchant Marine" I find the following:
Berne-Switzerland's dependence on foreign sources of supply for foodstuffs and for the raw materials for its industries has led to the creation of a Swiss merchant fleet. Without the fleet this country would, to a certain degree, suffer starvation and its industries would be severely crippled, in wartime, as they were in the world wars of 1914 and 1939.
And further down:
At the end of the last war, the Swiss people agreed that this fleet should be maintained and the confederation sold its ships to private shipping companies, which have gradually developed the Swiss merchant fleet. In June 1950, at the outbreak of the war in Korea, the fleet totalled 90,000 tons deadweight.

Supply-Transport
And then further:
The Swiss fleet comprises 33 ships totalling about 191 thousand tons deadweight, of which 20 have been built since 1948. The ships are modern and fast.
Why are these other nations adopting this policy of having a merchant marine? I submit it is because they know from experience that they must have their own ships. Is Canada to be the only nation taking the position that she has no need of a merchant navy? That is the problem. That is the question which must be faced by the government today. Time is running out. Unless something is done very quickly Canada will be in exactly that position, namely, that she has no deep-sea merchant navy.
We believe that there is still time to avert this disaster. We urge the government to have another look at this question. We urge them to bring about a change of policy. We believe that it will be one of the greatest tragedies in Canadian history if the Canadian merchant navy is allowed to disappear.
