speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is always a pleasure to discuss the estimates of the Minister of Transport because he always supplies us with a most comprehensive statement. I was very pleased to hear him announce tonight that he was interested enough in the Canso causeway to have had a recent look at it. Of course he was always interested in it, much more so than a lot of people who are claiming credit for that job.
I am glad that he had a recent look at it. I did also. It is about 85 per cent completed. It is a big undertaking and one that was long overdue. I know that when the minister goes down there within the next year or so to open that bridge-by the way I named it some time ago in the house as the Chevrier causeway-he will appreciate how important it is. Both he and I know that many difficulties that would never have been gotten around were overcome because of his own interest and faith in the project at a time when others were claiming it was an engineering impossibility, merely a visionary dream and simply a piece of old-time politics.
Nevertheless it is a reality there today and will serve a most useful purpose. The island of Cape Breton contains one-third of the total population of Nova Scotia and it is the largest industrial section east of Montreal. The transportation bottleneck that existed held back its development for many years. I am confident that when the causeway is completed and the bottleneck removed it will do a lot for the economic future of that island.
I am glad to hear also that the contracts for the diversion of the road and the construction of the lock on the Cape Breton side have

been let. I know the minister is going to be quite proud of that project some day and that day is not too far away.
I should like to say a few words on another item which I think is quite close to these estimates, and I refer to the St. Lawrence seaway. The minister is well aware that when this matter was under discussion a few months ago I was the only member who got up and voiced objection. When the Leader of the Opposition was welcoming the news that the United States had decided to come in and do their share of the project he said that every member of the house would welcome the announcement. I notice that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was a little more cautious when he said "nearly every member".
As far as I am concerned the matter is settled. I have sense enough to know there is no use continuing to fight after the referee has counted you out. You are not fighting any more, you are just imagining you are. First I should like to say that I would have been more pleased if Canada had decided to build the seaway alone. It would have been an indication that we were grown up, that we no longer found it necessary to get help from our grandmother.
I know the minister can tell me when he replies that an international agreement is necessary and that a certain amount of that work has to be done on the other side of the line. Nevertheless, we could have done that job ourselves. But now that we have the United States as a partner, and of course that matter is settled, there is no use of beating it any farther. I would say this: If we had built that seaway ourselves-it is a good project in this time of recession; it is a good project in the light of the fact that we have around 10 per cent to 12 per cent of our working force unemployed; at least it is going to give some employment-the tolls paid by foreign shipping and by United States ships would have liquidated its cost in the years to come.
We could have done the job ourselves. It would have been an indication that we were getting a little independent and capable of standing on our own feet. It would have indicated that we were able to develop anything that it was necessary to develop in this country.
I took objection to the seaway as a member from the maritimes because I knew that it was not going to help the economy of the maritime provinces at all. First, it makes the iron ore deposits of Ungava and Labrador much more readily available to the steel plants of the United States. Secondly, I am convinced that if the seaway were not built

many of the steel industries both in the United States and Canada would have to shift to the Atlantic coast, because that is the logical place in which to turn out raw steel. Lots of labour is available there; your coal is there; all the ingredients necessary to turn out raw steel are on the Atlantic coast. Your iron ore deposits are close at hand, and it would not be necessary to haul your coal and your raw materials across the country to have the raw steel turned out some place else. I am convinced that the seaway prevented the development of basic steel both in Canada and in the United States.
I know that it will also open up a waterway for United States coal, and of course competition for maritime coal is difficult at the present time. Maybe a little more because of the seaway will not do it very much harm. As far as the seaway is concerned I am pleased with one thing. During all the time that I was in opposition to it I said that our opposition was not unalterable; that if the St. Lawrence seaway was viewed in Canada as the Tennessee valley project was in the United States it would be a great boon to the country. The Tennessee valley project was a government project. It is worked on a co-operative basis. That great development in the United States stands out as perhaps one of the greatest co-operative developments financed by a government in the history of the world.
I was sceptical as to whether it might take place in Canada, but I notice in the press that there is a possibility of the Minister of Transport becoming the first chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. First, I hope we do not lose him from the House of Commons. He is a valuable man. He does a good job. But if anyone is to head the St. Lawrence seaway authority and the minister is the first chairman it will nullify a lot of my doubts about it because having worked with him I know, and every hon. member knows, that he is a pretty co-operative chap. He will go along where things are reasonable. In case they do make him chairman I hope that when he is working out the details of the power projects at Niagara and in the state of New York he will take the position that if we are to do this job in the interests of all of Canada, and if the seaway is to benefit the whole of Canada, the maritimes must not be forgotten.
Many hon. members said it would benefit the whole of Canada. Western members said it would move more grain at a cheaper rate. Of course we will have to take the railways up if we replace all the traffic that goes over the roads. Hon. members said it would benefit the whole of Canada; it
Supply-Transport
would open Canada up. Well, when the minister sets in to work out the details of power in the province of Ontario I hope he will remember that in addition to any power project that is contiguous to the St. Lawrence seaway, that is within reasonable reach and whose costs are not prohibitive, there is also a power project in New Brunswick that the people there have been asking for, for a good many years.
That, too, is a project that will require United States co-operation. My information is that the United States has been ready for quite a long while at least to discuss the matter. I refer to the Passamaquoddy project. The minister will become quite familiar with it after he takes over his new duties. He will say: we told the members of the House of Commons and the people of Canada that this was a great national project and that we were all going to pay our share of it. It was going to benefit the whole of Canada. If Ontario is entitled to power- and of course they are paying for it, they are doing the job themselves, but without the St. Lawrence seaway authority being set up and the assurance that the federal government was going to push the project, I do not think that power would have been touched. You have to have federal co-operation. If we are to assist in the power project, then the minister will remember the power project in New Brunswick.
In my opinion there is not a province in Canada that needs power more than does New Brunswick. A lot of mineral development and so forth could take place in that province if they had the power. We, too, have a power problem. When I talked about the St. Lawrence seaway the first time nothing very much was done about it. Within recent months the federal government has sent an expert into Nova Scotia to consider the possibilities of thermo-power developed from coal. That is being worked at now.
When I talked about the seaway, part of my argument was that if we were to support the St. Lawrence seaway by taxation then at least we were entitled to some kind of a survey in regard to the development of power from our basic resource of coal. That is being done. And since it is being done it modifies my disagreement with the St. Lawrence seaway. I trust it may work out as hon. members visualize it, and that it will benefit the whole of Canada; but I still have my reservations. They are somewhat relieved because of the rumour that the Minister of Transport may be the first chairman of the seaway authority. At least we have this assurance. He is the kind of person that I can walk in to see, sit down and tell

Supply-Transport
my troubles to and be sure of getting a sympathetic hearing. He is not going to be some import from some other part of the world, with a whole lot of hypothetical knowledge that I cannot understand, or cannot get in to see without having to get past a whole battery of secretaries.
Now I have your chin all fixed up I want to say a few words along the lines pursued by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. While he was talking he reminisced about the period during and after the war and he dealt at some length with the merchant marine. There can be no doubt that we are falling down on the job as far as the merchant marine is concerned, and our failure to protect our own coastal shipping is evident. I believe Canada is the only country in the world which permits foreign ships to come in and ply her coastal trade. That is taking place at the present time and, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra emphasized, a country which exports one-third of its total production must have a merchant marine service and, of course, in addition to that a good repair service. Our country must maintain its shipping yards so that they are adequate to repair our ships.
It would appear to me at the present time as though we did not have any ships of our own. What is the reason for that? I do not think the Canadian government is completely to blame. I believe that the people who have something to ship in this country are deliberately by-passing and sabotaging any possibility of developing a merchant marine in this country simply because they wish to use foreign ships. I think the reason for that also is that very low wages are paid on these ships. I will take my own end of the country as an example.
In 1939 the war broke out and the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation had the Dominion Shipping Company as a subsidiary with 12 or 14 boats of their own, and they employed Canadian seamen and paid Canadian wages. These boats were requisitioned and put into overseas service during the war, but since the war that fleet has not been built up. In fact, I do not think they own even two boats at the present time. I have here a clipping from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Wednesday of this week, and it points out the kind of difficulties into which we can fall. It states here that Dominion Steel and Coal have at least 12 boats carrying coal from Sydney to Montreal and they are all foreign-flag ships. The crew of one of these ships went on strike in Montreal recently because the wages being paid on that ship were as low as $90 per month. The crew was arrested because they refused to take the ship to sea. The crew of the next

ship which came into port went on strike in sympathy. Now the point I wish to make is this, that in a situation like that Canada has no authority. These are foreign-flag ships and if the crews of these ships go on strike in the port of Montreal there is nothing we can do about it because these men are subject to the laws of their own country, particularly in the matter of wages.
In the meantime the transportation of coal from Sydney to Montreal is tied up. There are eight other boats in that fleet which may be working under similar circumstances and we can get into a tangle there which may mean that shipments of coal up to Montreal will be tied up for the rest of the summer, and as far as we are concerned we have no authority to deal with that situation. Mind you, I want to say this for the benefit of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The reason why this company did not build up their own fleet, hire their own seamen and pay Canadian wages after the war was simply because they could get these foreign-flag ships for about one-third the cost and of course they found it cheaper to do it in that way. The result has been that our merchant fleet has gone down the drain right along the line. The government must take an equal share of the blame for not having a policy which would encourage the people who have freight to move by water across this country to build up a fleet, and a policy which would discourage the idea of lowering standards in this country and throwing our own sailors onto the beach.
If we are going to be patriotic I think we should start with ourselves. We should be loyal to our own institutions and to our own people, and if we are going to have wars every few decades we should try and remember some of our high sounding slogans rather than forget them as soon as the war is over. We must offer our people a better solution than we are doing at the present time, and instead of saying "You have got to lower your standards or you are going to become unemployed because you cannot compete with people who ship in vessels from countries where standards are very low", we should offer something much better.
This is not completely a government responsibility. It is the responsibility of everyone in this country. It is our responsibility as citizens to maintain our own standards and do what we can to raise the standards of others. I agree completely with the argument advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to the effect that we should encourage the building up of a merchant marine service in Canada, and we should encourage the training of merchant seamen in Canada.

If we just think back to the period during the war and at the end of the war we will no doubt recall that practically all the ships and officers who manned these ships were brought from the other side of the water. They had to be brought over here to operate our ships because between the wars we did what we are doing now, namely neglected to maintain a merchant service.
The only way we can maintain our standards is by driving it home to every Canadian that as citizens, regardless of what business they are in, it is their job to get standards up and not to lower them simply because for the moment they might be able to get something cheaper coming in from outside. I would point out, in addition, that no foreign ships are allowed to ply the coastal trade in the United States, Great Britain, or in any other country, but these foreign-flag ships can come into Canada and go from port to port throughout the country. When the St. Lawrence seaway is completed they will be able to take over all the shipping in this country.
The merchant fleet was the fourth arm of the services during the last war and there can be no doubt that the army, navy and air force would have starved to death in Britain if it had not been for the merchant seamen going across the Atlantic in convoys and delivering munitions, foodstuffs and everything which was required. I think we will be very shortsighted if we neglect to build up our merchant marine and I think it should be made quite clear that any corporation in this country which wants to use foreign-flag ships because they provide lower rates has an obligation to the people of this country to support our own merchant marine.
Another matter I would like the minister to consider when he is in conference with some of the people in the shipping repair industry in this country is that there are many small yards in this country, particularly in the maritimes, which grew up during the war when they were needed. The big yards can take care of themselves but these small yards, perhaps 50 or 60 in number and which are without very large facilities, could be used to repair many of our small ships. I would suggest to the minister that he might take a look at that section of his department some time because I am convinced that many of these yards that may be necessary in the future are not getting a fair share of the work. Many of them may be obliged to fold up. There was a time-and it may come again before long-when these yards were badly needed.
I agree with two things pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra with
Supply-Transport
regard to the re-thinking of this proposition of maintaining a merchant marine service in Canada. It is something that is absolutely essential and it is something that it should be possible to give to people who have freight to move from port to port in this country. I would ask the minister to remember this example I gave with respect to shipment of coal from Sydney to Montreal because it can be repeated. If that kind of thing develops there is not anything we can do about it. They are ships of another country in our ports. The season is short enough in the St. Lawrence in which to move coal up by water, and we should not lose any time about it.
I am not going to occupy any more time of the committee with general remarks. There are some things we shall have to say on the specific items as we reach them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since we are dealing with transportation tonight and as it goes hand in hand with development, I should like to say a few words in connection with railways and, in that connection, federal-provincial co-operation. If I appear to wander afield I hope you will bear with me because I assure you that what I have to say is all tied in with transportation.
In times past on many occasions the federal government has, I think, acknowledged the principle of co-operation between provincial and federal governments in respect of transportation. I suggest they have accepted the principle having regard to some of the projects which have been undertaken. In the maritimes there was the strait of Canso bridge for rail and road traffic in 1951 and the maritime marshlands rehabilitation project and so forth in 1948. There was also the Bow river irrigation project. I think we can readily see that the federal government has accepted the principle of co-operation between provincial and federal governments.
At this time I should like to comment for just a moment on the St. Lawrence seaway. A few days ago the Prime Minister indicated the willingness of Canada to "go it alone", as it were, in the matter of the expense of the St. Lawrence seaway. I think that that statement was well put, and I think to a great extent it gave the people of Canada much satisfaction in that it showed that we, as a Canadian government, were willing to take on a project of this size. The removal of the obstacles referred to by the Prime Minister in respect of United States participation in the St. Lawrence seaway is certainly a factor that we cannot overlook.
There is one other aspect I should like to mention just in passing. By reason of United States participation in the St. Lawrence seaway Canadians are going to be

Supply-Transport
saved the expenditure of a considerable amount of money. At least that is my hope. I think there is every reason to believe that we shall receive great benefit by the participation of the United States in the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. If there is a great deal of saving in respect of the building of the St. Lawrence seaway owing to United States participation, I feel that a good place to spend some of that money would be out in the province of British Columbia.
After all, British Columbia is located a long way from the St. Lawrence seaway. We believe that a fair share of the tax money should be spent in transportation facilities within that province. As I have the thing figured out in my mind, the St. Lawrence seaway will benefit those provinces from Saskatchewan east and perhaps Alberta to a small extent. But I feel that we in British Columbia are much in the same position as that in which the hon. member for Cape Breton South finds himself; we feel that the seaway possibly is not going to help us at all. By this I do not mean to suggest for a moment that we are against the building of the St. Lawrence seaway; we are for it. But at the same time we feel that we ought to be recognized by means of assistance in the development of our province through transportation facilities.
The British Columbia tax contribution to the federal government is extremely high. I think you will agree that this fact should have a great bearing on the consideration of the minister in this respect. In 1951-52 we find that the amount of corporation and personal income taxes and succession duties per capita in British Columbia was $199.88 as compared with the over-all Canadian figure of $152.74. In 1952-53 we find that the figure in British Columbia was $211.14 as compared with the over-all Canadian figure of $175.42. Canada then has a great deal of interest in the development of the great wealth of natural resources in British Columbia.
Since development is dependent on transportation, the first place to look for a chance to give that assistance to the province of British Columbia would be in the matter of increased transportation facilities within that province. The great Peace river area is badly in need of an outlet to the coast. In this area we have vast tracts of agricultural and forest land, as well as huge quantities of gas, oil and coal. The Pacific Great Eastern Railway is one place where this government could well place some of the money that it would save on the St. Lawrence seaway by United States participation.
[Mr. Leboe.l
We also have the new Japanese trade agreement, discussed in the house yesterday, which means increased trade from the west coast. Here again there is the necessity of adequate transportation facilities for the movement of carloads of agricultural and timber products from the central and northern parts of British Columbia. I understand from reading the press that the premier of British Columbia is now making application to the federal government for a contribution to extend the Pacific Great Eastern Railway from its terminus at Squamish into Vancouver, some forty miles, and from Prince George to Dawson Creek, some 274 miles.
I understand that one proposal is that the Canadian government, through the Canadian National Railways, should take over the Pacific Great Eastern, and that the other proposal is for a fifty-fifty participation in the railway itself. That would mean of course that a price would have to be set for the existing railway and that amount of money would have to be spent in extending it before the British Columbia government would take over its 50 per cent. The precedent of federal participation in the development of the provinces through the building of railways has been set on many occasions. We have the Kitimat line that is being built from Terrace to Kitimat in British Columbia. We have other railroads in Quebec and Ontario, and I see no reason why consideration should not be given to federal participation in the development of British Columbia through assistance in obtaining the railway facilities necessary for that development.
The question of providing access to the north country is one that affects other departments of the federal government, particularly the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. At the present time our provincial governments are faced with the problem of providing north and south highways, and the federal government, in its administration of the affairs of the northern territories, is dependent upon those highways. Therefore I think we have every reason to feel that consideration should be given to the request of the British Columbia government for assistance in the matter of railways.
I do not want to take up any more time. I think I have stated my case as clearly as I can tonight. However, I should like to say that I certainly agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Cape Breton South with respect to the Canadian merchant marine. They have spoken at some length, and I certainly agree

with what they have said. I should like the minister to show a spirit of good will towards the province of British Columbia and to view the matter from an absolutely fair point of view so far as the distribution of the tax dollar is concerned. British Columbia is a very lucrative place for the federal government to obtain tax money with which to carry on its affairs. We do not mind paying our share of taxes but we like to feel that in the spending of those tax moneys throughout Canada we are going to get a fair share.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in considering this first item of the estimates of the Department of Transport and in listening to the speeches that have been made by hon. members opposite, it is quite apparent what an important and varied department the Department of Transport is. I think hon. members recognize the very considerable responsibilities that are placed upon the shoulders of the Minister of Transport, and I think they likewise recognize the responsible manner in which the present minister has discharged these duties.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra spoke of a variety of matters, all of them important, as have the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I certainly have no wish to delay the committee in the consideration of this first item but there are several matters about which I wish to say a few words. There are a number of functions of the Department of Transport that are of great interest to all the people of the province of Nova Scotia, including the constituents of the constituency of Halifax which I, together with my colleague, have the honour to represent.
The marine services of the department are of course one of the vital functions which enter into the maritime life of Nova Scotia at every turn. I should like to compliment the minister on the manner in which the marine services of the department have been carried out over the past few years and the the very great strides that have been made by the minister and his officers in providing the aids to navigation required by the small fishing vessels and the large ocean-going vessels that use the various harbours of Nova Scotia. There has been a very extensive modernization of these aids to navigation. Radar has been applied to navigational problems. Aids to navigation have been quickly fitted with radar reflectors, and other steps have been taken to see that all vessels that have been equipped with modern equipment of this nature get the very best use out of it. I was interested to note in the last
Supp ly-Transport
annual report of the department that from the Halifax marine agency alone 231 lights of various classes are serviced and kept in operation in that area. This is a most essential and important contribution to the maritime life of the whole province of Nova Scotia. There is one point, however, that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and his officials for their consideration. I refer to the introduction of automatic equipment at locations where it is felt that the maintenance of a light tended by somebody who is responsible for the performance of the light is a matter of great importance. We recognize that in certain locations automatic equipment has definite advantages, and we should take note of those advantages. However, I would ask the minister to see that his officials consider each one of these cases in accordance with its special circumstances, and not to move too quickly in bringing into operation the use of automatic equipment where it really is not justified.
There is one other aspect of the operation of the marine service in Halifax that I feel deserves special mention at this time, and that is the administration of Sable island. This is a very specialized duty falling upon the department, the maintenance of the lighthouses, the communications station and the life-saving station on that island 100 miles off the coast of Nova Scotia which has become known as the graveyard of the Atlantic. I believe that the arrangements that have been made to maintain these services, to improve the buildings on the island and to improve living conditions there for the employees of the department who are required to live on that island all the year round, were very much needed. They have been carried into effect in a satisfactory manner. It is a most interesting life, I am sure, but a difficult life. I feel the department is to be congratulated upon the efforts that have been made to make the arrangements for the maintenance of these people as pleasant as it can be.
However, the one big remaining problem is the delivery of mail more regularly and on a more satisfactory basis. There have been suggestions with respect to the delivery of air mail to Sable island. I know that there are administrative and other difficulties in the way, but I would suggest to the minister that the matter be given careful consideration to see if it is not possible to improve the conditions of life on the island in this additional respect.
I want to say something with respect to the very important matter of pilotage services. As the minister knows, after the

Supply-Transport
end of world war II there were a number of rather difficult problems in connection with pilotage services in the port of Halifax as well as in some other ports in Canada. I am glad to report to the house and the minister, as I think he already knows, that by and large I believe these problems have been efficiently and satisfactorily met by the minister and his officials. I believe there is a very much better understanding between the active pilots and the officials who are responsible for the administration of the pilotage policy in the department. The main questions, with respect to the provision of pilot boats and the difficulties arising out of the superannuation fund, have been very largely met. There may be a continuing problem with respect to superannuation, but certainly the very special problem we had in Halifax arising out of the unfortunate loss of the pilot boat Hebridean during the war has been met.
I understand that the active pilots regard the present situation as quite satisfactory. We appreciate the initiative the minister and his officials took to make the changes which were required, and I am sure that the efficiency and care with which the responsibilities of the pilotage service have been carried out over the last few years has been very gratifying to the minister. I noticed in the report for 1952-53 that in Halifax, for example, there were only eleven instances where there were any accidents causing even minor damage in connection with the movement of ships in the harbour. I believe that amounted to approximately one-third of one per cent of all the pilotage jobs performed during that year, which is a very excellent record indeed.
In connection with the port of Halifax, Mr. Chairman, I want to mention also the matter of the provision of port facilities at Halifax to handle general cargo as well as the grain cargoes which flow through that port. I believe the facilities have recently been very satisfactorily extended in so far as the elevator and storage space is concerned. The galleries have been modernized with the replacement of the old No. 1 wooden gallery by a steel gallery, but I should like to point out to the minister that if the movement of grain through the port of Halifax increases, as we hope it may, with the additional elevator space, we will require, and consideration should be given to, the installation of additional gallery facilities to create new berths which could handle grain cargo. I think that is not a matter which should be pressed for immediate decision. I know the minister and his officials will keep that in mind, and as

the need develops will be prepared to take whatever steps are required to meet that need.
In so far as general cargo is concerned, the volume of traffic through the port of Halifax this past winter season has been most satisfactory. As a matter of fact, the experience during the winter shows that there is quite a pressing need for some additional berthing facilities in the port. It is recognized that the provision of new deep-water berths is a job that cannot be attended to very rapidly. I hope that the minister and his officials are considering taking the necessary steps to have the pier A job undertaken and pressed to the construction stage as quickly as possible. However, before that can be done I think there will be a need for additional shed and berthing facilities.
One way in which the problem could be met rapidly, and with at least some satisfaction, would be the provision of a new steel shed on a portion of pier 9, which is at the deep-water section of the harbour and where several berths for coastal shipping at least could be made available. Then, with the necessary shed facilities, a number of coastal ships could be worked, leaving free for the larger ocean-going vessels the berths which are now taken up by these coastal vessels. I would hope that some steps can be taken immediately to have shed facilities provided at this location and that a long-range program will be undertaken at the same time.
The expenditures made on harbour facilities in Halifax through the national harbours board over the last two years have been quite substantial and the results obtained have been most satisfactory. During this winter we saw the benefit of those expenditures. I believe that since the end of world war II there has been expended in Halifax on new facilities in the way of capital account a total of $5,890,000. Up to the end of 1954 the amount spent on maintenance will be $2,220,000. Those are very substantial amounts. We recognize what has been achieved by these expenditures and we recognize that the provision of those facilities have made it possible for the port to handle the volume of business which was handled this year.
Fortunately during the past few years the volume of summer business has been increasing. The experience in the past year or so, which we hope will be the same this year, has shown the volume of summer business through the port to be at least 50 per cent of the business done during the winter season.

Another matter to which I should like to refer is the future of the Canadian National steamship service to the West Indies. I followed with considerable interest the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Cape Breton South in connection with the Canadian merchant marine. I agree without hesitation with the principle which they enunciated of the importance of the government doing everything it reasonably and properly can do to maintain at least a minimum of a Canadian flag deep-sea fleet.
However, I was struck by the fact that the Canadian National Steamships company, by its operation of the West Indies service, has given an example of the maintenance of a Canadian merchant marine in a most competitive field of deep-sea operations. I congratulate the Canadian National steamships and the minister upon the fact that the freight service afforded by the Canadian National steamships between the West Indies and the Atlantic ports of Canada has been maintained. The minister made it plain in the house during this session that the purpose is to continue and maintain that service.
Unfortunately the last two survivors of that famous fleet of "Lady" boats which provided such excellent passenger service between the Atlantic ports of Canada and the West Indies and South America were withdrawn from service last year. We were all sorry to see the "Lady" boats go, but apparently it was an inevitable step. However, from the point of view of the maintenance of trade between the maritime provinces of Canada and the West Indies, which is a most important aspect of the trade of the maritime provinces, a cargo service is most important. We congratulate the government upon having been able to maintain that service and we look forward with confidence to its continuation in spite of the great difficulties which Canadian merchant marine operators are finding in keeping Canadian ships on the trade routes of the world. The fact that the government and the Canadian National steamships have been able to keep their ships under Canadian registry, to employ Canadian crews, and to pay Canadian scales of wages is I think a real accomplishment. It shows that the will of the operator is an important factor in the problem of keeping the Canadian merchant marine on the seas.
In referring to Canadian National Railways operations I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the need for the extension of the Nova Scotian hotel in Halifax operated by Canadian National Railways. We
Supply-Transport
are glad to note that the Canadian National Railways are going to provide much-needed hotel facilities in Montreal which will form an important part of their operations in central Canada.
The Nova Scotian hotel has been one of the successful operating hotels of the Canadian National system ever since it was opened in the early thirties. I am sure that the minister is aware that last year Halifax had the highest percentage of occupancy of hotel rooms of any city in Canada. The facilities of the Nova Scotian and the other hotels in Halifax were taxed more than were the facilities of any other hotels in this country. There is a real need for additional hotel accommodation and I hope that the railway and the minister will consider the possibility of some extension to the Nova Scotian hotel.
Another matter of real importance to Halifax is, as the minister knows, the provision of a civilian airport to meet the needs of Trans-Canada Air Lines and other operators of civil air transport in the area. Over the past several years the department has conducted a careful and thorough weather survey in order to find the most favourable site for such an airport. We were pleased when the minister announced some weeks ago that the results of the weather surveys in the Kelly lake area were sufficiently favourable to justify a ground survey in order to establish the feasibility of constructing an airport at that point.
I hope that that survey will proceed as promptly as possible and I hope that as a result of the findings therefrom the department and the city of Halifax will be able to get together and negotiate an arrangement for the construction of that much-needed addition to the transportation facilities of the province of Nova Scotia, the city of Halifax and the surrounding communities.
The concluding matter that I want to mention this evening, Mr. Chairman, is in connection with the building of the causeway across the strait of Canso. This very beneficial and important project ds proceeding most satisfactorily. I had the privilege of visiting the scene of the operations late last fall and was taken over the whole project by the contractor's superintendent. It is really a most impressive work. The volume and weight of rock involved are somewhat staggering, and the progress being made was most satisfying.
I was delighted to hear the minister say this afternoon that the rock-fill dam portion of the work is proceeding ahead of schedule. To some extent that is because the tide and ice conditions in the strait during the winter

Supp ly-Transport
were not found to interfere with the operation as much as had been originally expected. The department is to be congratulated on its participation in the project and in the excellent co-operation which it is giving to the Nova Scotia department of public works and highways, which is jointly financing this great undertaking. It was known to be the ambition of our late premier, the Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, that on the opening of the causeway he would be able to lead one hundred pipers across this great new highway playing "The Road to the Isles". I do hope the minister will do what he can to see that when that great causeway is opened those one hundred pipers are there and perhaps he will lead them across, playing that great Scottish anthem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Before beginning my brief remarks this evening, Mr. Chairman, may I say it is significant that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has complimented you on your very fine presentation of the various estimates of the department. It was a pleasure to be able to line up generally the various expenditures that will be taking place.
As many may know, this coming Sunday, May 16, is "Battle of the Atlantic Sunday". That is the day when we pay tribute to the men of the Canadian navy and to the men of the Canadian merchant marine. It is appropriate that we are discussing the merchant navy tonight. I should like to go back to 1945 and review the picture. At the end of the war all countries were in an abnormal condition. We saw them all making plans for their future trade and merchant navies. Finland comes to my mind first. They had a very poor merchant marine. I know it was considered to be perhaps the oldest in the world. They have made great strides and now have one of the most modern merchant navies afloat. I think of the Irish boats, too, which come into Saint John. They have also increased the Irish line to quite a considerable extent. Germany also is now back in the business with a vengeance. I had the pleasure last winter of viewing a German ship in Saint John, and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that there are none finer at sea today. We also have heard in recent days of Russia making overtures to twenty different shipyards across the country in an effort to have some ships built here by us.
We know also of the position of the United States and Great Britain in respect to their merchant marines. But what is Canada's attitude today? After the war there were 176 ships in the Park Steamships lines. This was a crown corporation, and we all had

hopes that some ships would at least be continued in the post-war years. There are statements on record in the various reports of the Canadian maritime commission. The second report is significant in this regard. We also have statements of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that generally some effort would be made to continue a small fleet. But what is the position today? It is obvious that the government is scrapping our merchant fleet. The thing that annoys me more than anything is that they are not even scrapping it in a businesslike way.
A lot of statements have been made to the effect that there is no definite policy about Canada's merchant marine. I feel that there has been a definite policy right along, namely, they are not going to do anything about it.
I should like to review one or two points without being too repetitious, Mr. Chairman, in this respect. There is ample justification for a merchant marine in Canada. I think firstly of trade. We all know that trade and merchant shipping go together. If we are to be considered as a great trading nation we must have a worth-while fleet. Secondly, I also think of shipbuilding. It is important to me down in Saint John that we continue our great shipbuilding of the war years. To be building only a few naval vessels is not enough. When one travels around the world he finds it wonderful to be able to say: "There is a ship which was made in Canada, flying the red duster".
Thirdly, and I think the most weighty argument, is that of defence. During the last war we pooled our ships. The ships of all the allies were pooled into a corporation called the British war transport, and they had the allocation of the ships to needy places around the world. I understand that a plan similar to that is being considered by NATO today. We know from the last war and we know today that it is just like sitting down at the table for a game of cards. You have to be able to back up your hand, and if you want consideration in wartime you must have a merchant fleet.
I think of the training of personnel and the difficulty we had to place men on our merchant ships in the second world war. It takes at least three years to train men. We had to go to the United Kingdom for those personnel. We must continue to have a merchant fleet if only for the training of personnel.
Another thought that comes to my mind in defence is the business of naval escorts. We are building up a very proud fleet of naval escort vessels that are second to none

in the world; but I ask this question, Mr. Chairman: What are those vessels to escort? There must be some ships for them, and surely we want to go all the way and have some merchant ships of our own to escort.
I ask the question: Why have we no merchant fleet, or why is it dwindling away? There have been suggestions that seamen were the cause of our decline in the merchant navy. Various criticisms are made of the strike in the post-war years which crippled our fleet. I hold no brief for the seamen, but I do not think this was the cause. I do not think that the ship owners are entirely to blame. There have been charges of excess profits; but the basic trouble that we know is the high cost of operation of those ships at sea. Naturally it is owing to the fact that we have an artificially high standard of living in Canada. You cannot blame seamen who are going to sea wanting conditions similar to those of their friends at home.
It is an indisputable fact that we have high costs with which to contend, but there is one far more significant reason in my opinion, Mr. Chairman, which has not been dwelt upon by anyone this evening. I suggest the main reason we have not now a merchant fleet and have not had one since the war is that we are a nation of landlubbers. Ottawa reflects the national mind and no consideration has been given to our seafaring provinces. When the time arrives to build a Canadian railway and subsidize it we can do that very well, but when it comes to building a fleet then the people of central Canada who do not know or understand the sea cannot visualize the problems facing these provinces.
Our trade with Britain is an example of this attitude. We have lost our traditional United Kingdom markets, though our trade picture is not too bad at present. The traffic now is across the border and it is impossible to get anyone in the central provinces to listen to the fact that trade with the United Kingdom is a lost cause.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I thought of trying to obtain a piece of poetry which would present this case, but on reflection I decided the situation had gone too far. Those of us who live in Halifax and Saint John do not like to see foreign flags flying on all the ships in our harbours. I feel that if we had someone with a strong voice here in Ottawa to speak about these things then conditions might perhaps be better. The Minister of Transport is interested in the St. Lawrence seaway; the Minister of Agriculture is interested in wheat; but who have we in the cabinet here who is interested in the sea and the merchant navy? There is no one. I suggest that that
Supply-Transport
is the main reason why no consideration has been given to the establishment of a merchant navy.
I would like to draw to the minister's attention one other matter in connection with the subsidy which has already been mentioned this evening. I do not feel we should be alarmed about this subsidy and accept the suggestion that we are only throwing our money away. The only time since the war when our merchant fleet had a subsidy was in 1949, and I believe then there was a subsidy of $3 million on 37 vessels. Statements have been made in the press and elsewhere that this money was merely thrown away and that our fleet was at an end, but I would like to put on record, Mr. Chairman, that this subsidy led to $12 million in federal and provincial taxes, $16 million in wages paid to Canadians and the spending of $7 million on repairs in Canadian shipyards.
There is one other matter to which I would like to refer and that is that with atomic warfare changing the picture every day surely this is the time for us to make plans for a new modern fleet. We would be the first in the field in this connection. In that regard I would like to read a short excerpt from an article in the Globe and Mail dated February 13, 1954, written by William Sclater who has a merchant navy and R.C.N. background. He is considered an authority on modern sea warfare. The article is entitled "A-Subs Pose New Problems for Sailors" and it reads as follows:
Canada, which has been getting rid of her obsolete war surplus freighter fleet by sale and by transfer of some to British registry, with a proviso that they be returned to Canadian registry in the event of war emergency is in an excellent position to set about laying the foundation for a real modern merchant marine of her own, for the first time.
With her atomic resources, good shipyards, marine architects and designers, she has plentiful ability, nor is there any real lack of sea-minded Canadian youth to man a small merchant fleet. The coming of the St. Lawrence seaway is another factor. There is, too, the possibility that a modern properly operated merchant marine may do what previous attempts with obsolete ships failed to do, and that is pay its way.
With British seapower at its lowest ebb in centuries and our present reliance being placed in what, at the best, could only be described as a doubtful dependency upon the sea power of other nations for war emergency, the need for an efficient small merchant marine of our own, comprising perhaps 50 ships built in our own shipyards, so that they, too, may be maintained, and built to the requirements of war emergency, is now a paramount need in the interests of our national security.
I leave these thoughts with you, Mr. Chairman, on the merchant marine.
I would like now to refer briefly to the St. Lawrence seaway. I would not like to

Supply-Transport
say that we in the maritimes are unhappy about the seaway, but we are still wary and doubtful as to just what it will mean to us. I myself am a little bit disappointed that in our acquiescence to the seaway project we did not take a lesson from those in the New England states who lobbied for various compromises while we were rendering our full support. That may be the fault of our political system. It may be the fault of hon. members here or there may be other reasons, but I know that Senator Kennedy in Boston and Senator Margaret Chase Smith in Maine were able to bicker and lobby at that time and obtain considerable concessions for their own areas. I feel that as the St. Lawrence seaway project develops we should be given consideration in regard to the problems which we ourselves face.
There is one other matter the St. Lawrence seaway brings to my mind and I will be pressing the minister for some kind of statement. I would like to know what is planned in regard to this seaway during winter months. I have not seen very much in the press, with the exception of one article, in this regard and I am interested in the probability of keeping the St. Lawrence seaway open. We should have had an engineering report on that matter for though it is obvious that ships cannot go up the St. Lawrence today for danger of fresh water ice, we do want to know what the department plans in this regard.
I would like to say a word or two on the national harbours board as its operations apply to Saint John. We hope that the dredging which has been conducted in the past will be carried out in the same manner in future. There has been some difficulty lately in getting tankers into the city. I am not sure whether the difficulties arise in connection with the national harbours board's section of our port but I do hope dredging will continue in the same fine manner in which it has been conducted in the past.
Another matter is the fishing licences issued for the port and I am given to understand that the national harbours board has certain authority and rights regarding the auctioning of weirs in the harbour along the west side of the port. However, they are not authorities on fishing and they set arbitrary reserve prices for the weirs and consequently when the reserve price is not met the weirs are not used for the three-year term and they fall into decay. I feel that if these weirs are the responsibility of the national harbours board then they should be turned over to the Department of Fisheries where they can be administered to better advantage.
We are pleased to see that the Pugsley extension in Saint John is being continued.

It is much needed there and we hope that pretty soon we shall see some lovely gleaming sheds on this new Pugsley wharf. We are also pleased to note that a new lighthouse supply and buoy vessel is being lined up for Saint John. In that regard we note the consideration given to us.
I should like to mention a remark or two made this evening. In his remarks the hon. member for Cape Breton South said that the season in the St. Lawrence is short enough. I hope nobody will agree with that statement. The complaint we are making-and it is the one that I have made before-is that the season in the St. Lawrence is much too long now. The hon. member for Halifax also made a statement which I, coming from the maritimes, would not wish to be associated in any way. It was to the effect that they were satisfied with the traffic through their port. Please, Mr. Chairman, do not think that I am satisfied at all with any port traffic that we have in Saint John or anywhere in the maritimes.

speechtext:
Coming as I do from probably the greatest maritime city in Canada, I suppose I should say something on this item. Like most other members-at least those from the two coasts-I have been bombarded during the last two years with propaganda from those who want a subsidy for the building of a Canadian merchant marine. That may possibly be the best way of building a merchant marine in Canada. But having regard to what has been accomplished following both world wars by those who are asking for the subsidy, in my opinion we should look at the matter carefully before we provide the subsidy. We should know exactly how much that subsidy is going to cost. If the Canadian government is going into the merchant marine business it seems to me that it had better go into it as a government itself and run the thing rather than by giving handouts to others. I am getting a little bit tired of those who are always extolling the virtues of private enterprise but who the moment they get into any sort of difficulty run to the government for a handout. That is exactly what we are up against at the present time.
Following the war we had a fairly sizeable merchant marine. Possibly those ships were slow and they might have had other faults. But those ships were turned over to private enterprise at extremely favourable prices. If private enterprise were not able to make a success of the thing, when they had this subsidy, what hope have we that they can make a success with any subsidy within reason that this or any other government would give them?

It seems to me that the time has arrived, not only when we should but when we shall be obliged to look upon the economy of this country as a whole in its relation to that of other countries. If we are going to try to be self-sufficient in every part of our economy, where are we going to find the markets for the things that we produce naturally in great abundance and have to sell? For instance, if we are going to build and man all our own ships, Great Britain, to whom we look to sell our wheat, salmon, lumber and fruit, to that extent at least will have to look somewhere else for the purchase of those things because evidently we are not going to give her an opportunity to pay for those things in the only way in which she can pay for them.
A few years ago in Vancouver I, along with some other members of parliament, attended a meeting called by the shipbuilding workers. One of the resolutions moved at the meeting was to the effect that the federal government be asked to pass legislation providing that all Canadian ship repairs would have to be done in Canadian yards. Two other members of parliament besides myself were at the meeting. When they were asked for their opinion on the matter they said that they did not have any. When I was asked for my opinion I told them that I was opposed to the motion because the moment we began doing this sort of thing, other countries would retaliate by insisting that their ships be built in their yards. I said then the same thing as I say now, namely that if we expect other countries to buy our goods we shall have to give those countries an opportunity to provide us with the goods and services with which they can provide us.
We have come to the stage where we must adopt co-operation in economic matters not only in our domestic affairs amongst ourselves but amongst nations. The nations of the world will have to adopt co-operation instead of competition in economic matters. The mere suggestion now that Canada should subsidize a merchant marine is proof positive that private enterprise in this country cannot operate a merchant marine without government assistance. As I said before, every time industry gets into difficulties are we going to provide means, either by tariffs or by subsidy, to see that that industry is going to be self-sufficient or to stay in the competitive field? That is not competition at all.
I do not know what the government's intention is in this matter, but I would just offer to it the advice that before it subsidizes a merchant marine it should lay before the House of Commons a comprehensive plan of what that subsidy involves, showing not only
Supply
what it will be necessary to provide this year but what it will be necessary to provide in succeeding years. It might be desirable that we should run our own merchant marine. But let me say again that if every country today is going to make itself self-sufficient in those things in which it thinks it should be selfsufficient, or if we are going to make ourselves self-sufficient in all things, all we shall be doing is to make ourselves self-sufficient in poverty. That is not the way that we shall have to carry on from this point forward.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
